Chapter 2: Declarative Resource Management — The Engine of Platform Engineering

Platform Engineering is built on one foundational concept: declarative resource management. Instead of telling Kubernetes how to run your app (imperative), you declare what you want (declarative) — and the platform makes it happen, keeps it that way, and heals it when things break. This chapter explains why declarative management is the non-negotiable core of every Internal Developer Platform, using our anihpj/jobpost Django app for every example.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📋 Declarative 🎯 Domain 1: 36% ☸️ Kubernetes YAML

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The fundamental difference between declarative ("what you want") and imperative ("how to do it") — and why platforms MUST be declarative
  • ✅ How every Kubernetes resource follows the same universal structure: apiVersion + kind + metadata + spec + status
  • ✅ When to use kubectl apply vs kubectl create — the three-way merge that makes GitOps possible
  • ✅ Why YAML won the configuration war over JSON — comments, anchors, readability
  • ✅ Infrastructure as Code (Terraform/Tofu) — the declarative pattern applied to cloud resources
  • ✅ Git as the single source of truth — every platform change is a Git commit with audit trail and rollback
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Platform Engineering Core Fundamentals 36% Foundation for GitOps (Ch 15-16) Foundation for CRDs & Operators (Ch 17-20)
⚠️ Declarative Thinking Is Tested Across ALL Domains

The CNPA exam doesn't just test WHAT declarative means — it tests your ability to APPLY declarative thinking to platform design. Key exam patterns to master:

  • Identify declarative vs imperative scenarios — "Which of these deployments follows the declarative pattern?" — the answer is always the one using YAML manifests + kubectl apply
  • Self-healing mechanism — "A pod crashes. What happens?" — The controller reconciles actual state to desired state automatically. You don't need to SSH in and restart it.
  • GitOps prerequisites — "Which tool enables GitOps?" — GitOps REQUIRES kubectl apply (declarative), not kubectl create (imperative). ArgoCD syncs every 3 minutes; create would fail on the second sync.

2.1 Declarative vs Imperative — The Foundation of Everything

The single most important concept in cloud native computing: declarative management means you describe WHAT you want, not HOW to achieve it. Kubernetes — and by extension, every platform built on Kubernetes — is fundamentally declarative. This distinction is tested heavily on the CNPA exam.

📖 Key Definitions

Declarative: "I want 3 replicas of anihpj running version v1.2.3." You declare the desired end state. The system figures out HOW to reach it and continuously maintains it.

Imperative: "Start a container named anihpj-1 with image v1.2.3. Now start anihpj-2. Now start anihpj-3. Now check if anihpj-1 crashed. If yes, restart it." You specify exact steps. If anything goes wrong, you must detect it and fix it manually.

The Restaurant Analogy — Why Declarative Wins

The easiest way to understand this distinction:

❌ IMPERATIVE (How)

"Go to the kitchen. Get a pan. Heat it to 350°F. Add 2 tablespoons of oil. Take 200g of pasta..."

Problems: If the chef leaves, nobody knows what step comes next. If the pasta burns, nobody knows whether to restart from scratch. Each command depends on the previous one succeeding.

✅ DECLARATIVE (What)

"I want pasta arrabbiata — spicy, al dente, with parmesan. Serves 2."

Benefits: Any chef can make it. If the pasta burns, the chef automatically starts a new batch. The end state is clear — the HOW is up to the chef.

anihpj Deployment — Imperative vs Declarative Side-by-Side

IMPERATIVE vs DECLARATIVE — anihpj Deployment Comparison
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ IMPERATIVE WAY                          ✅ DECLARATIVE WAY  │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ kubectl run anihpj-api    │          │ $ kubectl apply  │ │
  │  │   --image=anihpj:v1.2.3    │          │   -f anihpj.yaml │ │
  │  │   --port=8000               │          │                  │ │
  │  │   --replicas=3              │          │ replicas: 3      │ │
  │  │   --namespace=anihpj-prod  │          │ image: anihpj:v1 │ │
  │  │                             │          │ port: 8000       │ │
  │  │ # Later: scale up           │          │ namespace:       │ │
  │  │ $ kubectl scale             │          │   anihpj-prod    │ │
  │  │   deployment anihpj-api     │          │                  │ │
  │  │   --replicas=5              │          │ All in Git ✅     │ │
  │  │                             │          │ Self-healing ✅   │ │
  │  │ # What if pod crashes?      │          │ Idempotent ✅     │ │
  │  │ → YOU must notice and       │          │ Auditable ✅      │ │
  │  │   manually restart it       │          │ Rollback =       │ │
  │  │                             │          │   git revert     │ │
  │  │ # Who changed replicas?     │          │                  │ │
  │  │ → Unknown. No record. ❌     │          │                  │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────┘          └──────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The 5 Pillars of Declarative Management — Why Platforms Need It

🔄
1. Self-Healing

Declare "I want 3 replicas." A pod crashes → controller sees actual (2 pods) ≠ desired (3 pods) → creates a new pod automatically. No human intervention needed. This is impossible with imperative commands — you'd need a monitoring script that runs kubectl run whenever it detects a crash.

🔁
2. Idempotency

kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml run 1 time = run 100 times = same result. If the desired state already matches actual state, nothing happens. This is critical for GitOps — ArgoCD syncs every 3 minutes. Imperative commands would fail on repeated runs.

📋
3. Audit Trail

Every change is a Git commit: who changed what, when, and why. git log shows the complete history. Imperative kubectl commands leave no record — "who changed replicas from 3 to 5 at 2 AM?" Nobody knows. SOC2 and PCI-DSS auditors REQUIRE this audit trail.

🔙
4. Rollback

Bad deploy? git revert HEAD~1 → ArgoCD auto-reverts the cluster to the previous good state. With imperative commands, you'd need to remember ALL the commands that were run and reverse them in the correct order — practically impossible in production.

🤝
5. Collaboration

Declarative configs in Git = PR reviews. Alice proposes "scale anihpj to 5 replicas." Bob reviews the YAML diff, approves. Imperative commands = "Alice ran kubectl scale at 2 AM from her laptop." No review, no approval, no safety net.

💡 The CNPA Mindset Shift

Many newcomers ask: "Why can't I just run kubectl commands to manage my cluster?" The answer: platforms must scale to dozens of teams and hundreds of services. You cannot scale imperative commands across 50 developers. Someone will run the wrong command. Someone will forget to document a change. Someone will break production at 3 AM with no audit trail. Declarative management eliminates ALL of these failure modes by making Git the single source of truth and letting controllers handle the HOW.

The Declarative Philosophy Applied Beyond Kubernetes

Declarative thinking isn't just for Kubernetes — it's the foundation of all modern infrastructure management. The CNPA exam expects you to recognize the declarative pattern wherever it appears:

☸️
Kubernetes

Declare: "I want 3 replicas of anihpj:v2 with 250m CPU each."
Controller does: Schedules pods, monitors health, replaces failures.
Declarative in: Deployments, Services, Ingresses, CRDs, Operators.

🏗️
Terraform / Tofu

Declare: "I want a VPC with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16, a PostgreSQL RDS, and an EKS cluster."
Terraform does: Provisions, updates, or destroys resources to match.
Declarative in: .tf files = desired infrastructure state.

🚀
ArgoCD (GitOps)

Declare: Git repo contains all K8s manifests for all environments.
ArgoCD does: Continuously syncs cluster to match Git. Reverts drift.
Declarative in: Git = desired state. Cluster = actual state. ArgoCD = reconciler.

🛡️
Policy as Code (Kyverno)

Declare: "All pods MUST have resource limits. All images MUST come from our registry."
Kyverno does: Validates every pod creation against these rules. Blocks violations.
Declarative in: Policy YAML = desired governance state.

Real-World Horror Story — Why Imperative Commands in Production Are Dangerous

This actually happened at a mid-size SaaS company. Names changed to protect the guilty:

😱 The 3 AM Outage — An Imperative Nightmare
  • 3:00 AM: On-call engineer Sarah gets paged — anihpj production is down. Database connection pool exhausted.
  • 3:05 AM: Sarah runs: kubectl edit deployment anihpj-api — changes DB pool from 20 to 50. Pods restart. Site recovers.
  • 3:10 AM: Sarah goes back to sleep. She does NOT update the Git repo. "I'll do it tomorrow."
  • 3:13 AM: ArgoCD syncs. Detects the cluster has DB pool = 50, but Git says DB pool = 20. ArgoCD reverts the change. DB pool goes back to 20.
  • 3:15 AM: Database connection pool exhausted AGAIN. Site DOWN AGAIN. Sarah gets paged AGAIN.
  • 3:20 AM: Sarah runs the same kubectl edit command again. And again. And again — fighting ArgoCD's reconciliation every 3 minutes until she finally commits the change to Git.
  • Root Cause: Imperative command without Git commit. The platform's safety mechanism (ArgoCD) treated her fix as "drift" and reverted it.
  • Lesson: In a GitOps-managed platform, the ONLY way to make a persistent change is through Git. Imperative commands are temporary at best, destructive at worst.

The Physics of Declarative Systems — Why "What, Not How" Is a Law, Not a Preference

Declarative management isn't just a "nice pattern" — it's a fundamental property that emerges from control theory and distributed systems engineering. Understanding WHY it works at a deep level will help you reason about ANY platform tool:

THE CONTROL LOOP — The Universal Pattern Behind ALL Declarative Systems
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────┐                    │
  │                    │   DESIRED STATE      │                    │
  │                    │   (You declare this) │                    │
  │                    │                      │                    │
  │                    │   "replicas: 3"      │                    │
  │                    │   "image: anihpj:v2" │                    │
  │                    │   "cpu: 250m"        │                    │
  │                    └──────────┬───────────┘                    │
  │                               │                                 │
  │                    ┌──────────▼───────────┐                    │
  │                    │     COMPARATOR       │ ◄── Control Loop    │
  │                    │  "Does actual match  │                    │
  │                    │   desired?"          │                    │
  │                    └──────────┬───────────┘                    │
  │                               │                                 │
  │              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐               │
  │              │                │                │               │
  │     ┌────────▼──────┐  ┌─────▼──────┐  ┌──────▼──────┐       │
  │     │  ACTUAL <      │  │  ACTUAL =  │  │  ACTUAL >   │       │
  │     │  DESIRED       │  │  DESIRED   │  │  DESIRED    │       │
  │     │                │  │            │  │             │       │
  │     │  SCALE UP      │  │  DO        │  │  SCALE      │       │
  │     │  (create pods) │  │  NOTHING   │  │  DOWN       │       │
  │     │                │  │  (steady   │  │  (delete    │       │
  │     │                │  │   state)   │  │   pods)     │       │
  │     └────────┬───────┘  └─────┬──────┘  └──────┬──────┘       │
  │              │                │                │               │
  │              └────────────────┼────────────────┘               │
  │                               │                                 │
  │                    ┌──────────▼───────────┐                    │
  │                    │     ACTUATOR         │                    │
  │                    │  (API Server PATCH)  │                    │
  │                    └──────────┬───────────┘                    │
  │                               │                                 │
  │                    ┌──────────▼───────────┐                    │
  │                    │   ACTUAL STATE       │                    │
  │                    │   (Controller writes │                    │
  │                    │    this back to      │                    │
  │                    │    etcd via status)  │                    │
  │                    └──────────┬───────────┘                    │
  │                               │                                 │
  │              ┌────────────────┘ (feedback loop)                │
  │              │                                                  │
  │              └─────► back to COMPARATOR ──────► (repeats)       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 This pattern appears EVERYWHERE:                            │
  │     • Thermostat: Desired temp → measure → heat/cool → measure  │
  │     • Cruise Control: Desired speed → measure → accelerate/brake│
  │     • Kubernetes: Desired replicas → count pods → create/delete │
  │     • ArgoCD: Git state → cluster state → sync/revert          │
  │     • Terraform: .tf files → cloud state → plan/apply          │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🔑 KEY PROPERTY: The system CONVERGES to desired state.        │
  │     It doesn't matter HOW you got off-track — the controller    │
  │     always brings you back. This is called "eventual            │
  │     consistency with continuous reconciliation."                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Idempotency — The Mathematical Property That Makes GitOps Possible

Idempotency is a mathematical concept: an operation is idempotent if applying it once has the same effect as applying it any number of times. Formally: f(f(x)) = f(x). This is THE property that makes declarative systems safe for automation:

OperationIdempotent?1st Run2nd Run1000th RunSafe for Automation?
kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml✅ YESCreates resourceNo-op (already exists)No-op✅ SAFE
kubectl create -f anihpj.yaml❌ NOCreates resourceERROR: AlreadyExistsERROR❌ UNSAFE
terraform apply✅ YESProvisions infraNo changes (state matches)No changes✅ SAFE
aws rds create-db-instance❌ NOCreates DBERROR or DUPLICATEERRORS❌ UNSAFE
git merge feature-branch✅ YESMerges commitsAlready up to dateAlready up to date✅ SAFE
mkdir /tmp/anihpj❌ NOCreates dirERROR: File existsERROR❌ UNSAFE

💡 CNPA Core Insight: Every operation in a platform MUST be idempotent. If it's not, you can't automate it in a reconciliation loop — because repeated runs will fail. This is why GitOps tools exclusively use declarative, idempotent operations.

Imperative Still Has Its Place — But NOT for Platform Management

Imperative commands are NOT bad — they're useful for debugging and exploration. The CNPA exam expects you to know when each approach is appropriate:

ScenarioUse Imperative?Why
Deploying anihpj to production❌ NOUse kubectl apply -f with YAML in Git
Quick debug: "What's in this pod?"✅ YESkubectl describe pod anihpj-abc123 — exploration, not management
Scaling during incident⚠️ TEMPORARYkubectl scale --replicas=10 buys time, then update Git YAML to make it permanent
Learning K8s concepts✅ YESkubectl run is great for learning. Switch to declarative for real work.
GitOps-managed cluster❌ NEVERArgoCD will revert your manual changes in 3 minutes!

2.2 Kubernetes Manifests as Declarative API Objects

Every single resource in Kubernetes — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Ingresses, CRDs, Operators — follows the same universal structure. Once you understand this pattern, you can read and write ANY Kubernetes manifest, even for resources you've never seen before.

📖 The Universal K8s Object Structure

Every Kubernetes object has exactly 5 top-level fields: apiVersion + kind + metadata + spec + status. The first four are YOUR responsibility (the desired state). The last one — status — is written by the controller (the actual state). This split between spec (you) and status (controller) is THE key design pattern that makes Kubernetes self-healing.

The K8s Object Anatomy — The Universal Pattern

KUBERNETES OBJECT ANATOMY — Every Resource Follows This Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  apiVersion: apps/v1        ← WHICH API group and version      │
  │  kind: Deployment           ← WHAT type of resource             │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  metadata:                  ← WHO is this? Names, labels, etc.  │
  │    name: anihpj-api                                             │
  │    namespace: anihpj-prod                                       │
  │    labels:                                                      │
  │      app: anihpj                                                │
  │      tier: api                                                  │
  │      owner: jobpost-team                                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  spec:                      ← WHAT YOU WANT (desired state)     │
  │    replicas: 3              ← "I want exactly 3 pods"           │
  │    selector:                                                    │
  │      matchLabels:                                               │
  │        app: anihpj-api                                          │
  │    template:                ← Pod blueprint (what each pod is)  │
  │      metadata:                                                  │
  │        labels: {app: anihpj-api}                                │
  │      spec:                                                      │
  │        containers:                                              │
  │        - name: api                                              │
  │          image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.3                  │
  │          ports: [{containerPort: 8000, protocol: TCP}]          │
  │          resources:                                             │
  │            requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}            │
  │            limits: {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"}              │
  │          readinessProbe:    ← Is this pod ready for traffic?    │
  │            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}                │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  status:                    ← WHAT IS (actual, controller writes)│
  │    replicas: 3              ← 3 pods exist                      │
  │    availableReplicas: 2     ← ...but only 2 are Ready yet       │
  │    conditions:                                                 │
  │    - type: Available                                           │
  │      status: "False"                                           │
  │      reason: MinimumReplicasUnavailable                        │
  │                                                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The spec/status Split — The Most Important K8s Design Pattern

This is the engine that makes Kubernetes self-healing. Understand this and you understand Kubernetes at its core:

THE RECONCILIATION LOOP — How spec/status Enables Self-Healing
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  📝 SPEC (Desired)                    🔍 STATUS (Actual)        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ You write this in    │            │ Controller writes this│   │
  │  │ your YAML file:      │            │ based on reality:    │   │
  │  │                      │            │                      │   │
  │  │ replicas: 3           │            │ replicas: 2           │   │
  │  │ image: anihpj:v2     │            │ image: anihpj:v2     │   │
  │  │ cpu: 250m            │            │ cpu: 180m used       │   │
  │  └──────────┬───────────┘            └──────────┬───────────┘   │
  │             │                                    │              │
  │             └──────────── COMPARE ───────────────┘              │
  │                             │                                   │
  │                     DIFFERENCE FOUND?                           │
  │                        │        │                                │
  │                      YES       NO                               │
  │                       │        │                                │
  │                  ┌────▼───┐  ┌─▼──────┐                         │
  │                  │ TAKE   │  │ DO     │                         │
  │                  │ ACTION │  │NOTHING │                         │
  │                  │(create │  │(sleep  │                         │
  │                  │ 1 pod) │  │ 3 min) │                         │
  │                  └────────┘  └────────┘                         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 This loop runs CONTINUOUSLY — every controller does it:     │
  │     • Deployment controller: replicas match?                   │
  │     • Node controller: nodes healthy?                           │
  │     • Job controller: job complete?                             │
  │     • YOUR custom operator (Ch 20): your logic here             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj Complete Deployment Manifest — Annotated Line by Line

Let's look at the actual anihpj Deployment manifest with every line explained. This is the YAML you'll use throughout this guide to deploy our Django app:

anihpj-api-deployment.yaml 
# ─── apiVersion: WHICH Kubernetes API ───
apiVersion: apps/v1          # The Apps API group, stable version
kind: Deployment              # This is a Deployment resource

# ─── metadata: WHO is this? ───
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api            # Unique name within this namespace
  namespace: anihpj-prod      # Logical grouping (dev/staging/prod)
  labels:                     # Key-value pairs for organization
    app: anihpj               #   Used by Services to find pods
    tier: api                 #   Used by NetworkPolicies to filter
    owner: jobpost-team       #   Used for cost allocation & ownership

# ─── spec: WHAT you want ───
spec:
  replicas: 3                 # "I want 3 pods running at all times"
  selector:                   # How the Deployment finds ITS pods
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api         #   Must match template.metadata.labels
  strategy:                   # How to update pods
    type: RollingUpdate       #   Gradual: new pod up → old pod down
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1             #   At most 1 extra pod during update
      maxUnavailable: 0       #   0 downtime (never go below 3 pods)

  # ─── template: Pod blueprint ───
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api       # MUST match spec.selector.matchLabels
    spec:
      # Security context for the pod
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true    # Never run as root
        runAsUser: 1000       # Specific non-root UID
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.3
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          protocol: TCP
        # Resource requests & limits
        resources:
          requests:           # Minimum guaranteed resources
            cpu: "250m"       #   250 millicores = 0.25 CPU core
            memory: "256Mi"   #   256 mebibytes
          limits:             # Maximum allowed resources
            cpu: "500m"       #   500 millicores = 0.5 CPU core
            memory: "512Mi"   #   512 mebibytes
        # Health checks
        readinessProbe:       # "Is this pod ready for traffic?"
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz    # Django health check endpoint
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 10  # Wait 10s before first check
          periodSeconds: 5         # Check every 5 seconds
        livenessProbe:        # "Is this pod still alive?"
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        # Environment from ConfigMap & Secrets
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: anihpj-config     # Non-sensitive config
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secrets    # DB password, API keys, etc.
💡 What Makes This "Declarative"?

This YAML file is a declaration of intent. It says "I want 3 pods, each running anihpj:v1.2.3, each with a readiness probe on /healthz, each with 250m CPU." It does NOT say "first create pod-1, wait 30 seconds, then create pod-2..." That's Kubernetes' job. The Deployment controller reads this spec and continuously ensures reality matches it. If a pod crashes, the controller creates a new one. If you change replicas to 5, the controller adds 2 more pods. You declare. Kubernetes does.

How YAML Becomes a Running Pod — The Full Journey

Understanding what actually happens when you run kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml demystifies Kubernetes. Here's the complete flow — every step is automated by the platform:

Step 1: kubectl converts YAML → JSON

You write YAML. kubectl reads it, validates the structure, and converts it to JSON. Kubernetes API only speaks JSON. Time: milliseconds.

Client-side
Step 2: API Server receives the request

kubectl sends a POST (first time) or PATCH (subsequent applies) to the API server at https://k8s-api:6443/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/deployments/anihpj-api. Authentication (who are you?) and Authorization (are you allowed?) checks happen here.

API Server
Step 3: Admission Controllers validate

Before the object is stored, admission controllers run. Kyverno checks: "Does this deployment have resource limits? Is the image from our registry?" If validation fails, the request is REJECTED before anything is stored. If it passes, the object is written to etcd.

Admission
Step 4: Deployment Controller detects new/changed Deployment

The Deployment controller watches the API server for Deployment objects. It sees the new anihpj-api Deployment and reads the spec: "replicas: 3, image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.3." It creates a ReplicaSet object.

Controller
Step 5: ReplicaSet Controller creates Pods

The ReplicaSet controller sees its spec says "3 pods." It creates 3 Pod objects via the API server. The Scheduler notices these Pods have no node assigned and assigns them to healthy worker nodes based on resource availability.

Controller
Step 6: Kubelet starts the containers

The kubelet on each worker node receives the Pod assignment. It pulls the container image from the registry, creates the container with the specified resources, starts the readiness probe, and reports status back to the API server.

Node
Step 7: Readiness → Service → Traffic

When the readiness probe passes (/healthz returns 200), the Pod is marked "Ready." The Service controller adds this Pod's IP to the Service's endpoint list. The Ingress controller routes external traffic to the Service. anihpj is LIVE!

Live!

💡 Every step is declarative and automated. You never SSH into a node. You never manually start a container. The controllers handle everything — continuously, 24/7.

Common K8s API Resources — What a Platform Engineer Must Know

The CNPA exam covers a broad set of Kubernetes resources across all 6 domains. Here's a quick-reference table of the most important ones — every resource follows the same apiVersion + kind + metadata + spec pattern:

Resource (kind)apiVersionWhat It DoesCNPA Domain
Deploymentapps/v1Manages replica Pods with rolling updates. The workhorse of stateless apps.1 — Core Fundamentals
Servicev1Stable network endpoint (ClusterIP) for pods. Load balances traffic.1 — Core Fundamentals
ConfigMapv1Non-sensitive configuration data (env vars, config files).1 — Core Fundamentals
Secretv1Sensitive data (passwords, tokens, keys). Base64 encoded; use with encryption at rest.2 — Security
Ingressnetworking.k8s.io/v1HTTP/HTTPS routing to Services. External traffic entry point.2 — Security
NetworkPolicynetworking.k8s.io/v1Firewall rules between pods. "anihpj-db only accepts traffic from anihpj-api."2 — Security
PersistentVolumeClaimv1Requests storage (like a disk) for stateful workloads like databases.1 — Core Fundamentals
ServiceAccountv1Identity for pods. Used with RBAC to grant API access permissions.2 — Security
CustomResourceDefinitionapiextensions.k8s.io/v1Extends K8s API with YOUR resource types. Foundation of Operators.4 — APIs
HorizontalPodAutoscalerautoscaling/v2Auto-scales pods based on CPU/memory or custom metrics.3 — CD

💡 Pro Tip: Run kubectl api-resources to see ALL available resource types in your cluster. Every one follows the same apiVersion/kind/metadata/spec pattern.

Labels, Annotations, and Selectors — The Metadata That Powers Kubernetes

Kubernetes uses metadata to organize, filter, and connect resources. Understanding the difference between labels and annotations is a CNPA exam topic:

🏷️
Labels — Used for SELECTION and GROUPING

• Purpose: Identify and group objects for queries, filtering, and operations.
• Used by: Services (to find pods), Deployments (to manage pods), kubectl (to filter).
• Example: app: anihpj, tier: api, env: prod
• Restrictions: Must be 63 chars max, alphanumeric + hyphens + underscores. No special characters in values.
• CNPA relevance: Labels are how controllers FIND their resources. A Service uses label selectors to know which pods to send traffic to.

📎
Annotations — Used for METADATA and TOOLING

• Purpose: Store non-identifying metadata for tools, humans, and automation.
• Used by: kubectl (last-applied-configuration), cert-manager (certificate renewal), Ingress controllers (routing rules).
• Example: kubernetes.io/change-cause: "Scale to 5 replicas for Black Friday"
• Restrictions: Can be much larger than labels. Unstructured data like JSON is fine.
• CNPA relevance: kubectl apply stores its last-applied configuration as an annotation — this is literally how the three-way merge works.

YAML — Labels vs Annotations in Practice 
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod

  # LABELS: Used to SELECT and GROUP objects
  labels:
    app: anihpj              # Service uses this to find pods
    tier: api                # NetworkPolicy uses this to filter traffic
    env: production          # kubectl get pods -l env=production
    owner: jobpost-team      # Cost allocation, ownership tracking
    version: v1.2.3          # Canary deployments, A/B testing

  # ANNOTATIONS: Metadata for tools and humans
  annotations:
    # kubectl apply stores its last-applied config here:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"apps/v1","kind":"Deployment",...}

    # CI/CD pipeline records what triggered this deploy:
    ci.anihpj.io/deployed-by: "github-actions"
    ci.anihpj.io/commit-sha: "abc123def456"
    ci.anihpj.io/deployed-at: "2026-06-21T14:30:00Z"

    # Monitoring integration:
    prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
    prometheus.io/port: "8000"
    prometheus.io/path: "/metrics"

Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered — Why Kubernetes Controllers Are Different

This is an advanced concept that the CNPA exam touches on. Understanding it will make you a much better platform engineer:

❌ Edge-Triggered (Traditional Systems)

Reacts to EVENTS: "A pod crashed! Handle it!"

Problem: If the controller is down when the event fires, the event is LOST. The pod stays dead. This is why traditional monitoring systems miss alerts during outages — if the alert fires while PagerDuty is down, nobody gets paged.

Examples: Webhooks, event-driven architectures, traditional monitoring alerts.

✅ Level-Triggered (Kubernetes)

Reacts to STATE: "Right now, there are 2 pods. I want 3. Fix it."

Benefit: It doesn't matter if the controller was down when the pod crashed. When it comes back up, it sees the CURRENT state (2 pods) and reconciles to desired (3 pods). No events are lost because the system works on STATE, not EVENTS.

Examples: Kubernetes controllers, ArgoCD, Terraform (plan works on current state, not past events).

💡 Key Insight: Level-triggered reconciliation is why Kubernetes is so resilient. A controller can crash for hours, restart, and immediately bring the cluster back to the desired state. It doesn't "remember" events — it just reads the current state and acts.

2.3 kubectl apply vs kubectl create — The Command That Makes GitOps Possible

These two commands look similar but behave fundamentally differently. Understanding this difference is critical for the CNPA exam — and for understanding why GitOps tools like ArgoCD can work at all.

📖 The Key Difference in One Sentence

kubectl create is imperative — it makes a single API call to CREATE a resource. If the resource already exists, it FAILS. kubectl apply is declarative — it computes a three-way diff and PATCHES only what changed. If the resource already exists, it UPDATES it. If nothing changed, it's a no-op.

The Three-Way Merge — How kubectl apply Works

kubectl apply doesn't just "overwrite" your resource. It performs a sophisticated three-way merge comparing three sources:

THE THREE-WAY MERGE — kubectl apply Internals
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  SOURCE 1:              SOURCE 2:              SOURCE 3:        │
  │  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐ │
  │  │ YOUR FILE    │      │ LIVE OBJECT  │      │ LAST-APPLIED │ │
  │  │ (desired)    │      │ (in etcd)    │      │ CONFIGURATION│ │
  │  │              │      │              │      │ (annotation) │ │
  │  │ replicas: 5  │      │ replicas: 3  │      │ replicas: 3  │ │
  │  │ image: v2    │      │ image: v1    │      │ image: v1    │ │
  │  │ cpu: 500m    │      │ cpu: 250m    │      │ cpu: 250m    │ │
  │  └──────┬───────┘      └──────┬───────┘      └──────┬───────┘ │
  │         │                    │                     │           │
  │         └────────────────────┼─────────────────────┘           │
  │                              │                                 │
  │                     THREE-WAY DIFF                             │
  │                              │                                 │
  │    What changed since last apply?                              │
  │    • replicas: was 3 → now 5  (change in YOUR file)          │
  │    • image: was v1 → now v2    (change in YOUR file)          │
  │    • cpu: was 250m → now 500m  (change in YOUR file)          │
  │                              │                                 │
  │                ┌─────────────▼──────────────┐                  │
  │                │  API Server PATCHES only   │                  │
  │                │  the changed fields:       │                  │
  │                │  {replicas: 5, image: v2,  │                  │
  │                │   resources: {cpu: 500m}}  │                  │
  │                └────────────────────────────┘                  │
  │                                                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why apply Is REQUIRED for GitOps

This is one of the most important CNPA concepts — and a guaranteed exam topic:

apply vs create — GitOps Compatibility
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  KUBECTL APPLY (Declarative) ✅                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml    # 1st run: CREATED      │ │
  │  │ $ kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml    # 2nd run: no-op (same) │ │
  │  │ $ kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml    # 100th run: no-op      │ │
  │  │                                                            │ │
  │  │ ✅ SAFE for ArgoCD (syncs every 3 minutes)                 │ │
  │  │ ✅ SAFE for CI/CD pipelines                                │ │
  │  │ ✅ Idempotent: run 1 time = run 1000 times                 │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  KUBECTL CREATE (Imperative) ❌                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ kubectl create -f anihpj.yaml   # 1st run: CREATED      │ │
  │  │ $ kubectl create -f anihpj.yaml   # 2nd run: ❌ ERROR!    │ │
  │  │ Error from server (AlreadyExists):                         │ │
  │  │   deployments.apps "anihpj-api" already exists             │ │
  │  │                                                            │ │
  │  │ ❌ CANNOT be used in GitOps reconciliation loops           │ │
  │  │ ❌ ArgoCD sync would fail on every sync after the first    │ │
  │  │ ❌ CI/CD pipeline would break on repeated runs             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When to Use Which — Quick Reference

ScenarioUseReason
Deploying via GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux)applyIdempotent — safe for repeated syncs
CI/CD pipeline deploymentapplyPipeline runs on every push — must not fail on existing resources
One-time namespace creationeithercreate is simpler for truly one-time operations
Quick test pod for debuggingcreatekubectl run --rm -it debug --image=busybox
Applying a ConfigMap changeapplyUpdates existing ConfigMap without deleting and recreating
Platform management (your job)applyALWAYS use apply for platform resource management
⚠️ CNPA Exam Trap — The "I'll Just Use kubectl create in My Script" Fallacy

The exam will present scenarios where a developer suggests using kubectl create in a loop or pipeline. The correct answer is ALWAYS "use kubectl apply instead" — because create is not idempotent and will fail on any resource that already exists. This is why GitOps tools universally use apply semantics.

kubectl diff — Preview Changes BEFORE Applying

A critical command for platform engineering: kubectl diff shows you what WOULD change if you ran kubectl apply, without actually changing anything. This is like terraform plan for Kubernetes:

Shell — kubectl diff (Preview Mode) 
# Before applying, see what will change:
$ kubectl diff -f anihpj-api-deployment.yaml

diff -u -N /tmp/LIVE-123 /tmp/MERGED-456
--- /tmp/LIVE-123
+++ /tmp/MERGED-456
@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@
   replicas: 3
   template:
     spec:
       containers:
       - name: api
-        image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.2  # OLD version
+        image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.3  # NEW version
         resources:
           requests:
-            cpu: "250m"
+            cpu: "500m"  # Increased for performance

# ✅ Shows EXACTLY what will change when you apply
#    No surprises. Review the diff, then apply.

# This is the K8s equivalent of "terraform plan"
# Use it in CI: kubectl diff fails → PR needs review
# Use it locally: kubectl diff before every apply
💡 Platform Engineering Best Practice

Integrate kubectl diff into your CI pipeline. When a developer opens a PR that changes K8s manifests, the CI runs kubectl diff -f . against the staging cluster and posts the diff as a PR comment. Reviewers can see EXACTLY what infrastructure changes will happen BEFORE merging. This is the same pattern as terraform plan in infrastructure CI.

Server-Side Apply — The Next Evolution of Declarative Management

Kubernetes 1.16+ introduced Server-Side Apply (SSA) — a more sophisticated approach to declarative management that tracks field ownership. While client-side apply (the traditional kubectl apply) works well, SSA solves a critical problem: field conflicts when multiple controllers manage the same object.

CLIENT-SIDE APPLY vs SERVER-SIDE APPLY
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  CLIENT-SIDE APPLY (Traditional)                                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. kubectl reads the live object from the API server       │ │
  │  │ 2. kubectl computes the three-way diff LOCALLY             │ │
  │  │ 3. kubectl sends a PATCH to the API server                 │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ Problem: kubectl doesn't know WHO owns each field          │ │
  │  │ If HPA changed replicas and YOU changed replicas,          │ │
  │  │ kubectl can accidentally REVERT the HPA's change          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  SERVER-SIDE APPLY (SSA) — kubectl apply --server-side          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. kubectl sends the FULL desired object to the API server │ │
  │  │ 2. API server tracks FIELD OWNERSHIP:                      │ │
  │  │    • "replicas" field owned by: HPA (if HPA is active)    │ │
  │  │    • "image" field owned by: platform-team                 │ │
  │  │    • "resources" field owned by: platform-team             │ │
  │  │ 3. If HPA owns replicas, YOUR apply CANNOT change it      │ │
  │  │ 4. Conflicts are detected and reported — no silent reverts │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WHEN TO USE SSA:                                               │
  │  • Multiple controllers manage the same object (HPA + GitOps)  │
  │  • Large teams where field conflicts are likely                │
  │  • Programmatic clients (operators, controllers)               │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl apply --server-side -f anihpj.yaml                  │
  │  $ kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f anihpj.yaml│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💡 CNPA Note: While SSA is not heavily tested on the CNPA exam, understanding it demonstrates deep Kubernetes knowledge. The traditional kubectl apply (client-side) is still the primary exam topic.

2.4 YAML vs JSON for Declarative Configuration

Kubernetes accepts BOTH YAML and JSON — but YAML is the standard for human-authored configuration. Understanding WHY helps you make better platform design decisions.

📖 The Critical Fact

Kubernetes stores everything as JSON in etcd. When you run kubectl apply -f anihpj.yaml, kubectl converts your YAML to JSON before sending it to the API server. YAML is the human-friendly input format; JSON is the machine storage format. They represent the SAME data — just differently formatted.

Why YAML Won the Configuration War

YAML vs JSON — Side-by-Side Comparison for K8s Configuration
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  YAML ✅ — Human-Friendly                        JSON ❌ — For Config│
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐│
  │  │ # Owner: platform-team         │    │ // NOT VALID JSON!       ││
  │  │ # Why: anihpj API deployment   │    │ // No comments allowed   ││
  │  │ # Updated: 2026-06-21          │    │ // Can't explain WHY     ││
  │  │                                │    │                          ││
  │  │ apiVersion: apps/v1           │    │ "apiVersion": "apps/v1", ││
  │  │ kind: Deployment               │    │ "kind": "Deployment",    ││
  │  │                                │    │                          ││
  │  │ metadata:                      │    │ "metadata": {            ││
  │  │   name: anihpj-api            │    │   "name": "anihpj-api"   ││
  │  │                                │    │ },                       ││
  │  │ spec:                          │    │ "spec": {                ││
  │  │   replicas: 3                 │    │   "replicas": 3          ││
  │  │                                │    │ }                        ││
  │  │ • Comments explain WHY         │    │ • ❌ NO comments          ││
  │  │ • No braces or quotes noise    │    │ • Braces, brackets,       ││
  │  │ • Indentation = structure      │    │   quotes everywhere       ││
  │  │ • Multi-line strings:          │    │ • Multi-line: "line1\n    ││
  │  │   command: |                   │    │   line2\nline3" 😱        ││
  │  │     line1                      │    │ • ❌ Trailing comma        ││
  │  │     line2                      │    │   breaks everything       ││
  │  │ • Anchors (&name, *name):      │    │ • ❌ No anchors — copy/    ││
  │  │   reuse config blocks          │    │   paste duplicates only   ││
  │  └────────────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘│
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE FLOW:                                                       │
  │  YAML → kubectl converts → JSON → API Server → etcd (as JSON)   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl get deployment anihpj-api -o json  # See stored JSON │
  │  $ kubectl get deployment anihpj-api -o yaml  # See as YAML    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

YAML Features That Make Configuration Manageable

💬
Comments (#)

YAML allows inline and block comments. This is THE killer feature for platform engineering — you can document WHY a config value exists: replicas: 5 # Increased for Black Friday traffic spike — Alice, Nov 2026. JSON has no comment support at all.

🔗
Anchors (& and *)

Define a config block once, reuse it everywhere: env: &db_env {DB_HOST: db.svc} — then all your services reference *db_env. Change the host once, everywhere updates. JSON requires copy-paste for every repetition.

📝
Multi-line Strings (| and >)

| preserves newlines (for shell scripts, config files). > folds lines into a single string (for long descriptions). JSON requires \n escape sequences — unreadable for multi-line content.

👁️
Human Readability

Indentation defines structure — no {} or [] noise. A 500-line YAML Deployment is READABLE. The same content in JSON is a wall of braces, brackets, and quotes that's nearly impossible to scan visually.

💡 Platform Engineering Best Practice

Always use YAML for human-authored configuration. Use JSON only when programmatically generating manifests (e.g., your CI pipeline generates a JSON patch). For everything else — K8s manifests, Terraform configs, ArgoCD Application CRDs, Kyverno policies — YAML is the industry standard. The CNPA exam expects you to recognize YAML as the format for declarative K8s configuration.

YAML Gotchas — Common Pitfalls Every Platform Engineer Must Know

YAML's human-friendliness comes with trade-offs. These pitfalls cause real production incidents — the CNPA exam will test your ability to spot them:

⚠️ Gotcha 1: The "Norway Problem" — Unquoted Country Codes
  • The problem: YAML interprets NO as boolean false. If you write country: NO (for Norway), YAML reads it as country: false.
  • Also affected: YES, ON, OFF, TRUE, FALSE — all treated as booleans unless quoted.
  • Fix: Always quote potentially ambiguous values: country: "NO", version: "1.0" (without quotes, this becomes float 1.0).
⚠️ Gotcha 2: Indentation Sensitivity — Tabs vs Spaces
  • The problem: YAML forbids TAB characters. A single tab in your YAML file = parse error. This happens most often when copy-pasting from web pages or editors with mixed tab/space settings.
  • Symptom: Error: found character that cannot start any token or mapping values are not allowed in this context.
  • Fix: Configure your editor: "Insert spaces when tab is pressed." Use 2-space indentation for K8s manifests (the community standard).
⚠️ Gotcha 3: The Colon-in-Value Problem
  • The problem: image: ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1.2.3 is fine — one colon. But command: curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" has a colon in the VALUE, not as a key-value separator.
  • Fix: Quote the value: command: "curl -H \"Content-Type: application/json\"" — or use a multi-line string with |.

Managing YAML at Scale — Kustomize and Helm

Writing raw YAML for every environment doesn't scale. The CNPA exam covers two approaches to managing K8s configuration at scale:

AspectKustomizeHelm
How it worksTakes a BASE YAML + OVERLAYS → generates final YAML. No templates, no variables — just patches.Takes a TEMPLATE + VALUES → renders final YAML. Templates use Go templating with {{ .Values.xxx }}.
Built into kubectl?✅ YES — kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod❌ NO — requires helm install or helm template
Learning curveLow — works with plain YAML you already knowMedium — requires learning Go template syntax
Best forEnvironment-specific differences (dev vs prod replicas, resource sizes)Packaging and distributing complex applications with many configurable parameters
anihpj exampleBase: deployment.yaml. Overlay dev: replicas=1. Overlay prod: replicas=3.Chart with templates. helm install anihpj ./chart --set replicas=3
📖 CNPA Exam Focus

The CNPA exam primarily tests your understanding of Kustomize for configuration management — it's the native Kubernetes approach (built into kubectl) and aligns with the declarative, GitOps-friendly philosophy. You should understand the base/overlay pattern and how to use kubectl apply -k.

2.5 Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with Terraform/Tofu

The declarative pattern isn't limited to Kubernetes — it applies to cloud infrastructure too. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means declaring your VPCs, databases, load balancers, and DNS records the same way you declare your Deployments and Services: as code in Git.

📖 What is IaC?

Infrastructure as Code is the practice of managing cloud infrastructure through machine-readable definition files rather than clicking through a cloud console. "I want a PostgreSQL RDS instance with 20GB storage" — NOT "click here, then here, select this dropdown, type this value..."

anihpj Infrastructure — Declared as Code

IaC — DECLARATIVE INFRASTRUCTURE FOR anihpj
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  # anihpj/infra/main.tf — INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE               │
  │                                                                 │
  │  # ─── Network Layer ───                                       │
  │  resource "aws_vpc" "anihpj" {                                  │
  │    cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"                                   │
  │    enable_dns_support   = true                                  │
  │    enable_dns_hostnames = true                                  │
  │    tags = { Name = "anihpj-vpc", owner = "platform-team" }      │
  │  }                                                              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  resource "aws_subnet" "anihpj_private" {                       │
  │    vpc_id            = aws_vpc.anihpj.id                        │
  │    cidr_block        = "10.0.1.0/24"                            │
  │    availability_zone = "us-east-1a"                             │
  │    tags = { Name = "anihpj-private-subnet" }                    │
  │  }                                                              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  # ─── Database Layer ───                                      │
  │  resource "aws_db_instance" "anihpj_db" {                       │
  │    engine              = "postgres"                             │
  │    engine_version      = "15.4"                                 │
  │    instance_class      = "db.t3.medium"                         │
  │    allocated_storage   = 20                                     │
  │    storage_encrypted   = true                                   │
  │    username            = var.db_username                        │
  │    password            = var.db_password  # From Secrets Mgr    │
  │    skip_final_snapshot = false                                  │
  │    backup_retention_period = 7                                  │
  │    tags = { Name = "anihpj-db", owner = "platform-team" }       │
  │  }                                                              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  # ─── EKS Cluster (Kubernetes) ───                            │
  │  resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {                          │
  │    name     = "anihpj-cluster"                                  │
  │    role_arn = aws_iam_role.eks_cluster.arn                      │
  │    version  = "1.32"                                            │
  │    vpc_config {                                                 │
  │      subnet_ids = [aws_subnet.anihpj_private.id]               │
  │    }                                                            │
  │  }                                                              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ terraform plan    # Shows: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy│
  │  $ terraform apply   # Creates VPC + Subnet + RDS + EKS        │
  │  $ terraform plan    # Shows: 0 to change (NO DRIFT!) ✅        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The IaC Workflow — Same Pattern as K8s Manifests

1
Write Code

Declare infrastructure in .tf files

2
Review

PR review like any code change

3
Plan

terraform plan shows what WILL change

4
Apply

terraform apply makes it reality

5
Detect Drift

terraform plan detects if someone changed infra manually

Terraform vs Crossplane — Both Declarative, Different Approaches

The CNPA exam expects you to know when to use each:

AspectTerraform/TofuCrossplane
How it worksCLI tool manages state file. terraform apply syncs cloud to code.K8s-native. Creates cloud resources via CRDs. Controller reconciles.
State storage.tfstate file (local or remote: S3, Terraform Cloud)Kubernetes etcd (as custom resources)
Best forInitial cluster provisioning (EKS, VPC, RDS)Self-service infrastructure for developers (via K8s API)
anihpj useProvision EKS cluster + RDS + VPC initiallyDevelopers self-serve databases via K8s kubectl apply
Drift detectionterraform planContinuous reconciliation loop (like K8s)
💡 CNPA Architecture Insight

Many platforms use BOTH: Terraform provisions the foundational infrastructure (clusters, VPCs, IAM). Crossplane handles in-cluster self-service provisioning (databases, buckets, queues) — giving developers a K8s-native API for infrastructure WITHOUT giving them Terraform access. This layered approach is the recommended pattern for CNPA.

Terraform State — The "Source of Truth" for Your Infrastructure

Terraform maintains a state file (terraform.tfstate) that maps your declared resources to what actually exists in the cloud. Understanding state is critical — it's how Terraform knows what to create, update, or destroy:

TERRAFORM STATE — How terraform plan Works
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  STEP 1: terraform plan                                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  YOUR CODE (.tf files)          STATE FILE (.tfstate)     │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────┐  │ │
  │  │  │ resource "aws_vpc"   │      │ aws_vpc.anihpj: {    │  │ │
  │  │  │   cidr = "10.0.0.0"  │      │   id: "vpc-abc123",  │  │ │
  │  │  │ }                    │      │   cidr: "10.0.0.0/16" │  │ │
  │  │  └──────────┬───────────┘      │ }                     │  │ │
  │  │             │                  └──────────┬───────────┘  │ │
  │  │             │                             │              │ │
  │  │             └───────── COMPARE ────────────┘              │ │
  │  │                          │                                │ │
  │  │              ┌───────────▼───────────┐                   │ │
  │  │              │ DIFFERENCE?            │                   │ │
  │  │              │ No diff → DO NOTHING   │                   │ │
  │  │              │ New resource → CREATE   │                   │ │
  │  │              │ Changed field → UPDATE  │                   │ │
  │  │              │ Removed from code → DESTROY│                │ │
  │  │              └───────────────────────┘                   │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⚠️  STATE FILE BEST PRACTICES:                                  │
  │  • Store state REMOTELY (S3 + DynamoDB lock) — NEVER locally    │
  │  • State contains SECRETS (DB passwords) — encrypt it!          │
  │  • Use state LOCKING — prevents 2 people from applying at once  │
  │  • Never edit state manually — terraform import if needed       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ terraform {                                                  │
  │      backend "s3" {                                             │
  │        bucket  = "anihpj-terraform-state"                       │
  │        key     = "prod/terraform.tfstate"                       │
  │        encrypt = true                                           │
  │        dynamodb_table = "terraform-lock"  # Prevents race conds │
  │      }                                                          │
  │    }                                                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Terraform State — The "Do Not Lose This" File

If you lose your state file, Terraform doesn't know what it already created. Running terraform apply with an empty state will try to CREATE resources that already exist — resulting in conflicts, duplicate infrastructure, or worse. ALWAYS store state remotely with backups enabled. And NEVER store state files in Git — they contain secrets.

Terraform Resource Lifecycle — Create, Read, Update, Delete (CRUD)

Every Terraform resource goes through a lifecycle. Understanding this helps you predict what terraform apply will do:

TERRAFORM RESOURCE LIFECYCLE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────┐    terraform apply    ┌──────────────┐          │
  │  │ NOT IN   │ ────────────────────► │  CREATED     │          │
  │  │ STATE    │                       │ (in state)   │          │
  │  └──────────┘                       └──────┬───────┘          │
  │                                            │                   │
  │                              terraform plan│                   │
  │                              (detects drift)│                  │
  │                                            │                   │
  │                              ┌─────────────▼────────────┐     │
  │                              │   RESOURCE EXISTS        │     │
  │                              │   State matches code?    │     │
  │                              └──┬────────────┬──────────┘     │
  │                                 │            │                 │
  │                             YES │            │ NO (drift)      │
  │                                 │            │                 │
  │                         ┌───────▼──┐    ┌───▼──────────┐     │
  │                         │ DO       │    │ terraform    │     │
  │                         │ NOTHING  │    │ apply updates│     │
  │                         │ (steady  │    │ resource to  │     │
  │                         │  state)  │    │ match code   │     │
  │                         └──────────┘    └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  terraform destroy OR removed from code                    │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐                                         │ │
  │  │  │  DESTROYED   │ ← terraform state marks as destroyed     │ │
  │  │  │ (removed     │    Resource deleted from cloud           │ │
  │  │  │  from state) │                                         │ │
  │  │  └──────────────┘                                         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⚠️  CRITICAL COMMANDS:                                         │
  │  $ terraform plan     # PREVIEW: what will change?             │
  │  $ terraform apply    # EXECUTE: make reality match code       │
  │  $ terraform destroy  # DELETE: remove ALL managed resources    │
  │  $ terraform state rm # DANGER: remove from state (not cloud!) │
  │  $ terraform import   # ADOPT: bring existing resource into IaC │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Terraform Modules — Reusable Infrastructure Building Blocks

Just like you don't write the same function in every Python file, you shouldn't copy-paste the same Terraform code for every environment. Modules enable reusability:

📦
What Is a Terraform Module?

A module is a container for multiple resources that are used together. Instead of copying 50 lines of VPC configuration for every project, you write it ONCE as a module and reuse it with different inputs.

anihpj example: A postgres-db module that creates RDS + security group + backup policy. Used by 5 different services — each with different instance sizes.

🔧
Module Structure

modules/postgres-db/
├── main.tf (resource definitions)
├── variables.tf (input parameters)
└── outputs.tf (return values)

Usage: module "anihpj_db" { source = "./modules/postgres-db" instance_size = "db.t3.medium" }

Terraform vs OpenTofu — Understanding the Fork

In August 2023, HashiCorp changed Terraform's license from MIT to BSL (Business Source License). The community responded by creating OpenTofu — a fully open-source fork. The CNPA exam may reference both:

AspectTerraform (HashiCorp)OpenTofu (Linux Foundation)
LicenseBSL (restrictive for competitors)MPL 2.0 (fully open source)
GovernanceHashiCorp (single vendor)Linux Foundation (community-driven)
CompatibilityOriginal sourceDrop-in replacement — same .tf files, same commands
Commandterraform plan/applytofu plan/apply
CNPA ExamThe exam uses "Terraform/Tofu" language — both are valid answers. Know the difference but don't overthink it.

2.6 Git as the Single Source of Truth — The Foundation of GitOps

Every declarative configuration — K8s manifests, Terraform files, Kyverno policies, Backstage catalog definitions — lives in Git. This is not a "best practice" — it's the architectural foundation that makes GitOps, audit trails, rollbacks, and compliance possible.

📖 Git as Source of Truth = GitOps Prerequisite

When Git is the single source of truth, the cluster is always a reflection of what's in Git. If someone manually edits a resource with kubectl edit, ArgoCD detects the drift within 3 minutes and automatically reverts it to match Git. This means: the ONLY way to change production is through a Git commit. Every change is reviewed, approved, and recorded.

The anihpj Platform Repository Structure

GIT AS SOURCE OF TRUTH — anihpj/platform Repo Structure
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  GitHub Repository: github.com/anihpj/platform                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  /apps/anihpj/              ← Application manifests       │ │
  │  │    /base/                   ← Common K8s configs           │ │
  │  │      deployment.yaml        ← Deployment spec              │ │
  │  │      service.yaml           ← ClusterIP Service            │ │
  │  │      ingress.yaml           ← NGINX Ingress rules          │ │
  │  │      configmap.yaml         ← Non-secret environment vars  │ │
  │  │      kustomization.yaml     ← Kustomize base definition    │ │
  │  │    /overlays/dev/           ← Dev environment overrides    │ │
  │  │      kustomization.yaml     ← patches for dev              │ │
  │  │      replica-count.yaml     ← replicas: 1 (dev)            │ │
  │  │    /overlays/prod/          ← Prod environment overrides   │ │
  │  │      kustomization.yaml     ← patches for production       │ │

  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  /infra/terraform/          ← Infrastructure as Code       │ │

  │  │  /backstage/                ← Developer portal config      │ │
