Branching Strategy Comparison — When to Use Which

StrategyBranch LifetimeMerge FrequencyDORA LevelBest For
Trunk-Based DevelopmentHours to 1 dayMultiple times/dayElitePlatform engineering. ArgoCD GitOps. CNPA recommended.
GitHub FlowDaysEvery few daysHighSmall teams (2-5). Simple apps. No complex release process needed.
GitFlowWeeksEvery few weeksLowLegacy apps with scheduled releases. NOT recommended for cloud native.

💡 CNPA Choice: Trunk-Based Development for ALL platform repos. GitHub Flow for small standalone projects. GitFlow is an anti-pattern for platform engineering — long-lived branches directly conflict with CI and GitOps principles.

CI Pipeline Timing Optimization — Why Stage Order Matters

CI stages should be ordered from FASTEST to SLOWEST, and from HIGHEST failure rate to LOWEST. This "fail-fast" ordering minimizes the time developers wait for feedback:

CI PIPELINE TIMING — Optimized vs Unoptimized Stage Order
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  OPTIMIZED ORDER (Fail-Fast) ✅                                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  LINT → TEST → BUILD → SCAN → SIGN → PUSH                │ │
  │  │  30s     2min    3min     1min    30s     1min            │ │
  │  │  30%     15%     5%       3%      0.1%    0.01%          │ │
  │  │  fail    fail    fail     fail     fail    fail           │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  WEIGHTED AVG FEEDBACK: ~1.5 min per failed pipeline      │ │
  │  │  If lint fails (30% chance): feedback in 30 SECONDS       │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  UNOPTIMIZED ORDER (Fail-Slow) ❌                               │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  BUILD → SCAN → TEST → LINT → SIGN → PUSH                │ │
  │  │  3min     1min    2min     30s    30s     1min            │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  WEIGHTED AVG FEEDBACK: ~4 min per failed pipeline        │ │
  │  │  If lint fails (30% chance): waits 6+ MINUTES!            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 DESIGN PRINCIPLE: Order by (speed × failure_rate) ascending│
  │     Fast + high-fail-rate FIRST. Slow + low-fail-rate LAST.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

6.8 Container Image Building in CI — Build → Tag → Scan → Sign → Push

Building container images in CI requires careful attention to tagging, security scanning, and signing. Each step is essential for a secure, auditable, GitOps-compatible pipeline:

Image Tagging Strategy — The 4 Types of Tags

Tag TypeExampleUse CaseMutable?Production-Ready?
Git SHAabc1234def5678Traceability to exact commit. Every CI build gets a unique SHA tag.❌ Immutable✅ YES
Semantic Versionv1.2.3Release management. Tags point to a specific, approved release.❌ Immutable✅ YES
Environmentstaging, productionKnow which image is deployed WHERE. ArgoCD uses these for promotion.⚠️ Mutable (moves)⚠️ WITH CAUTION
latestlatestDevelopment convenience. Always points to the most recent build.🔴 HIGHLY MUTABLE🔴 NEVER in production!

💡 CNPA Rule: Production manifests must ALWAYS use immutable tags (SHA or semver). Never use `:latest` or mutable environment tags in production. `:latest` is ambiguous — "latest" when? By whom? With what code?

The Multi-Stage Dockerfile — Optimize for CI

anihpj/Dockerfile (Multi-Stage Build) 
# ─── STAGE 1: BUILDER (Compile, collect static, install deps) ───
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

# Collect Django static files (run during build, not at runtime)
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ─── STAGE 2: FINAL (Minimal production image) ───
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Create non-root user (SECURITY: never run as root)
RUN groupadd -r anihpj && useradd -r -g anihpj anihpj

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only NECESSARY files from builder (not build tools)
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
COPY --from=builder /app .

USER anihpj
EXPOSE 8000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz')"

CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

Alternative Builders — Beyond Docker

📦
Kaniko — No Docker Daemon Needed

Builds container images INSIDE a Kubernetes pod without requiring a Docker daemon or privileged mode. Ideal for CI environments where Docker-in-Docker (DinD) is not allowed.

Usage: kaniko --context=git://github.com/anihpj/jobpost --destination=ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost:$SHA

🧱
Buildpacks — No Dockerfile Required

Auto-detects your language (Python) and builds an OCI-compliant image with best practices (layers, security, caching). No Dockerfile to write or maintain. Ideal for golden paths that auto-generate everything.

Usage: pack build ghcr.io/anihpj/jobpost --builder heroku/builder:24

Monorepo vs Polyrepo — Where Should Your Code Live?

✅ Monorepo (anihpj Approach)

One repo contains: All application code (apps/), infrastructure (infra/terraform/), policies (policies/), Backstage catalog (backstage/).

Pros: Cross-cutting changes in one PR. Easy to enforce org-wide standards. Single source of truth for ArgoCD.

Cons: Larger repo is slower to clone. PR conflicts between teams sharing the same files.

⚠️ Polyrepo (One Repo Per Service)

Separate repos: github.com/anihpj/api, github.com/anihpj/web, github.com/anihpj/infra, etc.

Pros: Teams are fully autonomous. Smaller, faster repos. No cross-team merge conflicts.

Cons: Cross-cutting changes require N PRs. Harder to enforce org-wide standards. ArgoCD must watch many repos.

💡 CNPA Recommendation: Start with monorepo for small-to-medium orgs (3-10 teams). Migrate to polyrepo when teams grow to 20+ and autonomy becomes critical. ArgoCD ApplicationSets can manage both.

CI/CD Tooling Comparison — What Powers Your Pipeline

The CNPA exam expects you to understand the CI/CD tooling landscape. Here's the comparison of the major options a Platform Engineer must evaluate:

ToolTypeBest ForKey StrengthKey Weakness
GitHub ActionsManaged SaaSTeams on GitHub. 90% of CNPA use cases.Deep GitHub integration. Massive marketplace. OIDC for cloud access.Vendor lock-in. Debugging failed workflows is hard. 6-hour job timeout.
GitLab CIManaged + Self-hostedTeams on GitLab. DAG-based pipeline needs.Integrated GitLab ecosystem. Auto DevOps. Powerful DAG pipelines.YAML config can become complex. Smaller marketplace.
JenkinsSelf-hostedLegacy orgs. Complex custom pipelines.Extremely flexible (Groovy). 1800+ plugins. No vendor lock-in.High maintenance burden. Plugins break on upgrade. Not cloud-native.
TektonK8s-nativeCloud-native platforms. CI as K8s pods.Fully K8s-native. CRD-based. No external dependency. Scalable.Steep learning curve. Less mature. Requires K8s cluster.
CircleCIManaged SaaSSpeed-critical. Excellent caching.Fast parallelism. Great caching. Good for monorepos.Expensive at scale. Less integrated than GitHub.

💡 CNPA Pick: GitHub Actions for most platforms (deep GH integration, zero infra). Tekton when fully K8s-native is required (CRD-based CI). Avoid Jenkins for NEW platforms.

6.9 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of platform goals, maturity models, build-vs-buy decisions, team structure, and CI fundamentals.

Core Fundamentals Q1 of 10
A platform provides developers with 5 different CI/CD tool options (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Tekton). Does this reduce cognitive load?
A) Yes — developers have more choices and can pick their favorite
B) No — 5 choices increases cognitive load. The platform should provide ONE opinionated CI/CD golden path
C) Yes, if each tool is well-documented
D) It depends on the team size
✅ Correct Answer: B — Too many choices = cognitive load

Cognitive load is about REDUCING the number of tools a developer must learn and choose from. Offering 5 CI/CD options forces every developer to evaluate, compare, and decide — that's cognitive load. The platform should provide ONE opinionated, well-designed golden path. Advanced users can have escape hatches, but the default should be singular and opinionated.

Core Fundamentals Q2 of 10
In the Platform Iron Triangle, which of these is a valid trade-off between SPEED and SECURITY?
A) Skip all security scanning to deploy faster
B) Require 3 manual security approvals before every deployment
C) Scan for CRITICAL and HIGH CVEs in CI (adding 2 minutes). Move MEDIUM CVE scanning to a weekly scheduled scan.
D) Disable CI entirely and manually review all code
✅ Correct Answer: C — Balanced trade-off

Option A sacrifices ALL security for speed (wrong). Option B sacrifices ALL speed for security (wrong — manual gates are anti-platform). Option C finds the BALANCE: critical security checks in CI (automated, fast), less-critical checks deferred to a weekly scan. This is the platform engineering approach: manage trade-offs intentionally, not absolutely.

Core Fundamentals Q3 of 10
A team has: self-service golden paths, ArgoCD GitOps, Backstage portal, and developers deploy to production without filing tickets. What Platform Maturity Level is this?
A) Level 1: Crawl
B) Level 2: Walk
C) Level 4: Fly
D) Level 3: Run (Self-Service)
✅ Correct Answer: D — Level 3: Run

Full IDP with portal + golden paths + GitOps + ticketless deploys = Level 3 (Self-Service). This is the CNPA target. Level 4 would add AI-driven features: predictive scaling, auto-remediation, AI incident response.

Core Fundamentals Q4 of 10
Your organization needs a database for the platform. You have no in-house database expertise. Which decision is correct?
A) BUY — Use AWS RDS (managed PostgreSQL). Databases are commodity infrastructure, not business differentiators.
B) BUILD — Write your own database management system to perfectly fit your needs
C) ADOPT — Run PostgreSQL yourself on Kubernetes with an Operator
D) Ask each development team to set up their own database
✅ Correct Answer: A — BUY managed database

Databases are commodity infrastructure. Unless database management IS your business (you're a database company), BUY the managed service. RDS handles: backups, failover, patching, monitoring, scaling — all undifferentiated heavy lifting. Your platform engineers should focus on golden paths and developer experience, not PostgreSQL backup scripts.

Core Fundamentals Q5 of 10
An organization has 200 developers across 15 teams. How many platform engineers should they have?
A) 2 — platform engineering is just automation, it scales infinitely
B) 8-12 — approximately 1 platform engineer per 15-25 developers
C) 50 — one platform engineer per 4 developers for dedicated support
D) 0 — developers should manage their own infrastructure (DevOps)
✅ Correct Answer: B — 8-12 platform engineers

The industry ratio is ~1 platform engineer per 15-25 developers. 200 ÷ 20 = 10 platform engineers. This team plus a product manager and an SRE can support 15 stream-aligned dev teams. Less than this → platform becomes a bottleneck. More than this → platform overhead costs outweigh the productivity gains.

Core Fundamentals Q6 of 10
Which CI pipeline stage order is correct and WHY?
A) Build → Scan → Test → Lint — build must happen first so tests run on the actual image
B) Scan → Build → Lint → Test — security scanning is most important
C) Lint → Test → Build → Scan — fastest and cheapest stages first. Fail fast to save pipeline time.
D) Test → Lint → Scan → Build — tests are the most valuable stage
✅ Correct Answer: C — Fastest/cheapest stages first

CI pipelines should FAIL FAST: run the quickest, cheapest stages first so developers get feedback ASAP. Lint (30 seconds) → Test (2 minutes) → Build (3 minutes) → Scan (1 minute). If lint fails, the developer knows in 30 seconds instead of waiting 6+ minutes for build+scan to complete. This ordering principle applies to ALL CI pipelines regardless of language.

Core Fundamentals Q7 of 10
A CI pipeline has code coverage configured to fail below 60%. A developer pushes code with 55% coverage. What happens?
A) The pipeline warns but passes — coverage is just a guideline
B) The pipeline passes and files a ticket to add more tests later
C) The pipeline deploys to staging anyway — coverage can be added later
D) The pipeline FAILS. The developer must add tests until coverage > 60% before merging.
✅ Correct Answer: D — Pipeline FAILS. Coverage is a HARD gate.

Code coverage thresholds in CI are HARD GATES — not suggestions. If the threshold is 60% and the code is at 55%, the pipeline FAILS. The developer cannot merge until they write additional tests or justify lowering the coverage threshold (via PR review). This is shift-left in action: catch insufficient testing BEFORE code reaches production.

Core Fundamentals Q8 of 10
A team using GitFlow has feature branches that live for 3-4 weeks. Their lead time from commit to production is 3 weeks. What should they change?
A) Switch to Trunk-Based Development — merge to main at least daily. Short-lived branches reduce integration pain.
B) Add more reviewers to feature branches to speed up approval
C) Keep GitFlow but automate the merge process
D) Move from weekly deploys to monthly deploys to reduce failure rate
✅ Correct Answer: A — Switch to Trunk-Based Development

Long-lived feature branches (3-4 weeks) are the ROOT CAUSE of slow lead time. Each week a branch lives without merging adds integration risk (merge conflicts, incompatible changes). Trunk-Based Development — merging to main at least daily — is the DORA-recommended practice that correlates with Elite performance (lead time < 1 hour).

Core Fundamentals Q9 of 10
Which image tag should a production Kubernetes manifest use?
A) image: anihpj/jobpost:latest
B) image: anihpj/jobpost@sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6...
C) image: anihpj/jobpost:production
D) image: anihpj/jobpost:stable
✅ Correct Answer: B — SHA256 digest (immutable reference)

SHA256 digests are the most specific, immutable reference to a container image. Even if someone pushes a new image with the same tag, the SHA256 digest will be different, protecting you from tag mutation attacks. `:latest`, `:production`, and `:stable` are all mutable tags that can point to different images at different times — NEVER use them in production.

Core Fundamentals Q10 of 10
Which statement best describes the relationship between CI and Platform Engineering?
A) CI is optional — platforms can work with manual testing if well-documented
B) CI replaces the platform — if you have good CI, you don't need an IDP
C) CI is only for application code — platforms don't need CI for infrastructure
D) CI is the FOUNDATION — platforms provide standardized CI golden paths so every team gets automated verification without building it themselves
✅ Correct Answer: D — CI is foundational to platform engineering

Without CI, every team builds their own verification pipeline — or (worse) deploys untested code. The platform provides standardized CI golden paths: lint → test → build → scan → sign → push. Every team gets this automatically when they create a service. CI is not an application concern — it's a PLATFORM capability that every golden path includes by default.

🟡 Part 2: Platform Observability, Security & ConformanceCNPA 20% · Ch 7-11

Chapter 7: Observability Fundamentals — Metrics, Logs, Traces & The Platform's Eyes

You can't fix what you can't see. Observability is the platform's sensory system — it tells you WHAT is happening (metrics), WHY it happened (logs), and WHERE the problem is (traces). Together they provide complete system visibility. Without observability, you're flying blind — deploying code into production with no way to know if it's working, failing, or about to fail. This chapter covers the three pillars of observability using Prometheus, Loki, Grafana, Tempo, and OpenTelemetry — all applied to our anihpj/jobpost Django app.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 📊 Observability 🎯 Domain 2: 20% 📈 Prometheus/Grafana

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The Three Pillars — Metrics (WHAT), Logs (WHY), Traces (WHERE) — and how they combine for complete visibility
  • ✅ Prometheus metric types — Counters, Gauges, Histograms, Summaries — with real anihpj examples
  • ✅ PromQL — the Prometheus Query Language for alerting and dashboarding
  • ✅ Loki + LogQL — label-based log aggregation that's cheap and Kubernetes-native
  • ✅ Distributed Tracing — following a request through anihpj-web → api → db → redis to find bottlenecks
  • ✅ Grafana dashboards — unified visualization for metrics, logs, and traces in a single pane of glass
  • ✅ OpenTelemetry — the CNCF standard for unified, vendor-neutral observability instrumentation
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Platform Observability & Security 20% Foundation for Platform Measurement (Ch 25-26) Foundation for Incident Response (Ch 13)
⚠️ Observability Is a PLATFORM Capability — Not an Afterthought

The CNPA exam tests observability as a platform design concern, not just as "install Prometheus." Key exam patterns to master:

  • Every golden path MUST include observability by default. When a developer creates a service via Backstage, Prometheus ServiceMonitor, Loki log parsing, and Grafana dashboards should be auto-provisioned. No opt-in required.
  • Know the metric types cold. Counter (http_requests_total) vs Gauge (cpu_usage) vs Histogram (request_duration). The exam will ask which metric type fits a given scenario.
  • Prometheus PULL model is different. Unlike Datadog/CloudWatch (PUSH), Prometheus reaches INTO your pods to scrape /metrics. This architectural difference affects network policy, service discovery, and scaling.

7.1 The Three Pillars of Observability — Metrics, Logs, Traces

Observability isn't one thing — it's three complementary data types that together answer every question about your platform's behavior. No single pillar is sufficient alone:

📖 The Three Pillars Defined

Metrics (WHAT) — Numerical measurements collected over time. "How many 500 errors occurred in the last 5 minutes?" Metrics are lightweight, cheap to store, and perfect for alerting. They tell you SOMETHING is wrong.

Logs (WHY) — Timestamped text records of discrete events. "The database connection timed out after 30 seconds with error 'too many connections'." Logs are detailed but expensive to store (full text). They tell you WHY something went wrong.

Traces (WHERE) — A record of a single request's journey through all services. "The request spent 320ms in the database query but only 2ms in Redis." Traces tell you WHERE the bottleneck is.

The Three Pillars — Visualized with anihpj Examples

THE THREE PILLARS OF OBSERVABILITY — Complete Picture
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  📊 METRICS (What?)              📝 LOGS (Why?)                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ http_requests_total     │    │ [2026-06-15 14:30:00]      │  │
  │  │   app="anihpj-api"      │    │ ERROR anihpj-api:           │  │
  │  │   status="500"          │    │ DB connection timeout       │  │
  │  │          = 47           │    │ at 10.244.2.10:5432         │  │
  │  │                         │    │ retries=3, max_retries=3    │  │
  │  │ cpu_usage_percent       │    │ stacktrace: File "db.py",  │  │

  │  │          = 82.3%        │    │                              │  │
  │  │                         │    │ Lightweight to store?  ✅    │  │
  │  │ request_duration_sec    │    │ Searchable by text?    ✅    │  │
  │  │   le="0.5"              │    │ Expensive at scale?    ⚠️   │  │
  │  │          = 1,234        │    └────────────────────────────┘  │
  │  │                         │                                    │
  │  │ Cheap to store    ✅     │                                    │
  │  │ Fast to query     ✅     │                                    │
  │  │ Perfect for alerts ✅    │                                    │
  │  └────────────────────────┘                                    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🔍 TRACES (Where?)                                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  TRACE ID: abc123def456 — Follows ONE request everywhere  │  │
  │  │                                                           │  │
  │  │  User Request: GET /api/jobs/                             │  │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │  │
  │  │  │ Span 1: anihpj-web    → 15ms  ✅                     │ │  │
  │  │  │ Span 2: anihpj-api    → 45ms  ✅                     │ │  │
  │  │  │ Span 3: anihpj-db     → 320ms ⚠️ SLOW! (bottleneck!) │ │  │
  │  │  │ Span 4: anihpj-redis  → 2ms   ✅                     │ │  │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │  │
  │  │  TOTAL: 382ms | BOTTLENECK: DB query = 84% of time!      │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 TOGETHER THEY TELL THE COMPLETE STORY:                      │
  │  • Metrics ALERT: "500 error rate spiked to 15% at 14:30!"     │
  │  • Logs EXPLAIN: "DB connection timeout — pool exhausted"       │
  │  • Traces PINPOINT: "The /api/jobs/ query to jobs table         │
  │    took 320ms — 8× longer than normal. Missing index?"         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Incident resolution WITHOUT all 3: Hours of guesswork.         │
  │  Incident resolution WITH all 3: Minutes of targeted action.    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Each Pillar Alone Fails — The "We Only Have..." Trap

Many platforms start with just ONE pillar and learn the hard way. Understanding these failure modes is critical for CNPA platform design — the exam will ask you to identify which pillar is missing from a scenario:

📊
Metrics-Only: You Know WHAT, Not WHY

"Error rate is 15%. P95 latency is 2.3s." You know there's a problem, but you don't know WHY (no stack traces from logs) or WHERE (no trace to pinpoint the slow service). You SSH into every pod guessing. The outage drags on for hours.

📝
Logs-Only: You Know WHY, Not SCALE

"DB connection timeout at 10.244.2.10." You found the error, but is it 1 request or 10,000? Without metrics, you have no idea of the blast radius. You fix the one error you found — but 500 others are still happening. Users keep reporting issues.

🔍
Traces-Only: You Know WHERE, Not IMPACT

Request abc123 spent 320ms in the DB query. You see one slow trace. But is 320ms normal? Is every request this slow? Without metrics, you can't compare to baseline. Without logs, you miss the underlying error. You optimized the wrong thing.

How the Observability Stack Physically Runs in Kubernetes

Understanding theory is one thing. Understanding deployment architecture is what CNPA tests. Here's how Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Promtail, OTel Collector, and Grafana actually run as workloads in your cluster:

OBSERVABILITY DEPLOYMENT ARCHITECTURE — K8s Workloads
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  OBSERVABILITY NAMESPACE (platform-monitoring)                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Prometheus│   Loki   │  Tempo   │ Grafana  │Alertmgr   │ │
  │  │  StatefulSet│Deployment│Deployment│Deployment│Deployment │ │
  │  │  2 rep, PV │ 2 rep, S3│ 1 rep, S3│ 2 rep    │ 2 rep     │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  PER-NODE (DaemonSets):  Promtail (log collector)               │
  │                          OTel Collector (telemetry router)      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  APPLICATION PODS: anihpj-api, anihpj-web, anihpj-db           │
  │  • Each pod exposes: /metrics endpoint (Prometheus scrapes)     │
  │  • Each pod writes: stdout/stderr (Promtail tails)              │
  │  • Each pod sends: OTLP traces to OTel Collector (gRPC)        │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 DEPLOYMENT DECISIONS (CNPA Tested):                         │
  │  • Prometheus → StatefulSet (needs persistent disk for TSDB)   │
  │  • Loki/Tempo → Deployment (stateless, backed by S3)           │
  │  • Grafana → Deployment (stateless, dashboards via ConfigMap)  │
  │  • Promtail → DaemonSet (one per node, tails /var/log/pods)    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Hospital Analogy — Understanding Observability Through a Familiar Lens

If Kubernetes observability feels abstract, think of it like a hospital. Every patient (request) generates three types of information — and doctors need ALL three to diagnose and treat effectively. A platform that only has metrics is like a doctor who only checks your heart rate — they know something is wrong but can't tell you what or why:

OBSERVABILITY AS A HOSPITAL — Metrics, Logs, Traces, Events
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  📊 METRICS = VITAL SIGNS (Heart rate, blood pressure, temp)    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  "Patient's heart rate is 150 BPM" (normal: 60-100)       │ │
  │  │  → You know SOMETHING is wrong, but not WHAT               │ │
  │  │  → Continuous, numerical, cheap to monitor                 │ │
  │  │  → K8s equivalent: "P95 latency = 850ms (normal: 200ms)"  │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  📝 LOGS = MEDICAL CHART NOTES (Doctor's observations)          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  "Patient reports chest pain, started 2 hours ago after   │ │
  │  │   eating. History of acid reflux. No shortness of breath."│ │
  │  │  → Detailed, timestamped, EXPLAINS the vital signs         │ │
  │  │  → K8s equivalent: "DB connection timeout at 10.244.2.10, │ │
  │  │    pool exhausted (100/100), retries=3"                   │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🔍 TRACES = DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING (X-ray, MRI, CT scan)          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  "MRI shows a blockage in the left anterior descending    │ │
  │  │   artery — that's why the EKG is abnormal."               │ │
  │  │  → Shows EXACTLY WHERE the problem is                     │ │
  │  │  → K8s equivalent: "The /api/jobs/search DB query took    │ │
  │  │    320ms — that's 84% of total request time."             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  📅 EVENTS = ADMISSION/DISCHARGE RECORDS                        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  "Patient admitted at 14:00. Transferred from ER to ICU   │ │
  │  │   at 14:30. Discharged at 18:00."                         │ │
  │  │  → State changes, contextual breadcrumbs                   │ │
  │  │  → K8s equivalent: "Pod scheduled 14:28 → Container       │ │
  │  │    started 14:29 → Readiness probe passed 14:30"         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE DIAGNOSIS WORKFLOW:                                     │
  │  Metrics (vital signs) alert: "Something is wrong!"            │
  │  Logs (chart notes) explain: "DB connection pool exhausted."   │
  │  Traces (imaging) pinpoint: "The slow query is on /api/jobs/." │
  │  Events (records) contextualize: "Deployment scaled down at    │
  │    14:28 — fewer DB connections available."                    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  A doctor with only vital signs? Guessing.                      │
  │  A doctor with all four? Precision medicine.                    │
  │  A platform with only metrics? Guessing.                        │
  │  A platform with all four observability signals? Precision      │
  │  incident response. This is what CNPA platform engineers build. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Observability Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

Learning what NOT to do is as important as learning what to do. These are the most common observability mistakes platform teams make — the CNPA exam will test your ability to RECOGNIZE these anti-patterns:

🚫
Dashboards Without Alerts

"We have beautiful Grafana dashboards!" But nobody watches them 24/7. The outage started at 3am and was discovered by a user at 9am. Fix: Every critical metric needs a PrometheusRule that fires an alert to PagerDuty. Dashboards are for INVESTIGATION, not detection.

🚫
Alerting on Symptoms of Symptoms

"CPU is at 85%!" But why? Is it serving more users (good) or stuck in an infinite loop (bad)? Alert on what USERS experience: error rate, latency, availability. CPU is a leading indicator but not a symptom. Alert on the symptom FIRST, use saturation for early warning.

🚫
Logs Without Structure

"2026-06-15 ERROR: Something went wrong with the database connection for user id=42." This is unparseable. Loki can't extract fields. Fix: Structured JSON logging. Every log line is a JSON object with typed fields. LogQL can query | json | user_id == 42.

🚫
Traces Without Context Propagation

You instrumented anihpj-api with OTel but forgot anihpj-web. Result: traces show anihpj-api in isolation — no connection to the original request. Fix: OTel auto-instrumentation on ALL services. Context propagation requires EVERY service in the chain to forward the traceparent header.

Events — The Fourth Signal (Beyond the Three Pillars)

The CNPA exam also covers Events — discrete records of state changes. Unlike metrics (continuous numbers) or logs (text messages), events capture "something HAPPENED at this specific moment":

📅
What Events Capture

• K8s Events: Pod Scheduled → Pulling → Running → Terminated
• Deployment Events: Scaled from 3→5 replicas. Rollback from v2→v1.
• CI/CD Events: Build #1247 started → passed → deployed
• Config Changes: ConfigMap "anihpj-config" updated by Alice

🔄
How Events Differ from Metrics/Logs

• Metrics: "CPU is at 82%" (continuous, right now)
• Logs: "DB connection timeout" (text, at a timestamp)
• Events: "Deployment scaled from 3→5" (state change, at a moment)
• Together: Events connect the dots — "CPU spiked BECAUSE deployment scaled down 5→2 at 14:29"

RED Metrics — The Minimum Viable Observability for Any Service

Every service on your platform should expose at minimum RED metrics. This is the CNPA golden path standard for observability:

📈
RATE — How many requests?

Metric: http_requests_total (Counter)
PromQL: rate(http_requests_total[5m])
Answers: "Is traffic normal? Did we just get a spike? Is the service being used at all?"
anihpj: 152 req/sec on /api/jobs/

❌
ERRORS — How many are failing?

Metric: http_requests_total{status=~"5.."} (Counter)
PromQL: rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])
Answers: "Is the service healthy? Error rate > SLO?"
anihpj: 0.3% error rate (well within 1% SLO)

⏱️
DURATION — How fast is it?

Metric: http_request_duration_seconds (Histogram)
PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
Answers: "Is the service slow? P95 latency within SLO?"
anihpj: P95 = 245ms (well within 500ms SLO)

7.2 Metrics with Prometheus — The Cloud Native Metrics Standard

Prometheus is the de-facto standard for cloud native metrics. It's a CNCF graduated project, used by virtually every Kubernetes platform. Understanding its architecture, data model, and query language is essential for the CNPA exam:

📖 Prometheus Architecture — The PULL Model

Unlike most monitoring tools that WAIT for data to be pushed to them, Prometheus PULLS metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints. Every 15-60 seconds, Prometheus reaches INTO your pods and fetches the /metrics endpoint. This PULL model has profound implications: your app must expose /metrics, Prometheus needs network access to every pod, and service discovery is built-in (Prometheus auto-discovers pods via K8s API).

Prometheus Architecture — How It All Fits Together

PROMETHEUS ARCHITECTURE — The PULL Model in Action
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │              PROMETHEUS SERVER                             │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ┌────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  │ │
  │  │  │  SCRAPER   │  │   TSDB   │  │  PROMQL ENGINE      │  │ │
  │  │  │  (pulls    │─▶│ (Time    │─▶│  (Query Language)   │  │ │
  │  │  │  /metrics) │  │  Series  │  │                     │  │ │
  │  │  │            │  │  DB)     │  │  rate(http_requests  │  │ │
  │  │  │  Every 30s │  │          │  │  _total[5m])        │  │ │
  │  │  └─────┬──────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┬──────────┘  │ │
  │  │        │                                   │             │ │
  │  └────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┘ │
  │           │ PULL (HTTP GET /metrics)          │ Query results   │
  │           │                                   │                 │
  │  ┌────────▼──────────┐              ┌─────────▼──────────┐    │
  │  │  anihpj-api Pod   │              │    ALERTMANAGER     │    │
  │  │  :8000/metrics    │              │  ┌────────────────┐ │    │
  │  │                   │              │  │ Alert Rules:    │ │    │
  │  │  http_requests    │              │  │ error_rate > 5% │ │    │
  │  │  _total{          │              │  │ → CRITICAL      │ │    │
  │  │    status="200"   │              │  └───────┬────────┘ │    │
  │  │  } = 45231        │              │          │          │    │
  │  └───────────────────┘              │  ┌───────▼────────┐ │    │
  │                                     │  │ PagerDuty      │ │    │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐              │  │ Slack #alerts  │ │    │
  │  │  anihpj-db Pod    │              │  │ Email on-call  │ │    │
  │  │  :9187/metrics    │              │  └────────────────┘ │    │
  │  │  (postgres        │              └─────────────────────┘    │
  │  │   exporter)       │                                         │
  │  └───────────────────┘                                         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY: Prometheus PULLS — it reaches INTO pods. Your app      │
  │     must expose a /metrics endpoint. Service discovery via K8s  │
  │     API means Prometheus auto-finds new pods — no config needed. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prometheus Metric Types — With Real anihpj Examples

The CNPA exam expects you to know the four Prometheus metric types and when to use each:

📈
Counter — Only Increases (or resets to 0)

Use for: Counting things that only go UP — total requests, errors, bytes sent.

anihpj example:
http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"} = 45231
"45231 total requests served since start."

Query: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) → requests per second. Always use rate() with counters — never the raw value.

📊
Gauge — Goes Up AND Down

Use for: Current values that fluctuate — CPU %, memory bytes, active connections.

anihpj example:
cpu_usage_percent{pod="anihpj-api-7"} = 82.3
"Right now, pod anihpj-api-7 is using 82.3% CPU."

Query: avg(cpu_usage_percent) → average CPU across all pods. No rate() needed.

📐
Histogram — Observations Bucketed by Value

Use for: Measuring distributions — request latency, response sizes. Most important for SLOs.

anihpj example:
request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"} = 8912
"8912 requests completed in ≤ 0.5 seconds."

Query: histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) → "95% of requests complete within X seconds."

📏
Summary — Client-Side Quantiles (Rare)

Use for: When you can't use histograms (limited use). Calculates quantiles on the CLIENT, not query time.

anihpj example: Not typically used — Histograms are preferred because quantiles can be calculated at query time.

CNPA Note: Histograms > Summaries in almost all cases. Summaries can't be aggregated across instances — a P95 of P95s is not the global P95.

PromQL — The Prometheus Query Language

PromQL is how you query Prometheus metrics to create dashboards and alerts. Here are the most important patterns you'll need for CNPA:

PromQL — Essential Queries for Platform Engineering 
# ─── RATE: Convert counter to per-second ───
rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"}[5m])
# → "How many requests per second over the last 5 minutes?"

# ─── ERROR RATE: Percentage of failed requests ───
rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api",status=~"5.."}[5m])
  /
rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"}[5m])
# → "What % of requests are failing? Alert if > 0.05 (5%)"

# ─── P95 LATENCY: 95th percentile request duration ───
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="anihpj-api"}[5m]))
# → "95% of requests complete within X seconds"

# ─── CPU SATURATION: Are we approaching limits? ───
rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}[5m])
  /
container_spec_cpu_quota{pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}
# → "What % of CPU limit is being used? Alert if > 80%"

# ─── MEMORY USAGE: Risk of OOMKilled? ───
container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}
  /
container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}
# → "What % of memory limit is in use? Alert if > 85%"

# ─── AVAILABILITY: Uptime percentage ───
avg(up{job="anihpj-api"} * 100)
# → up=1 means pod is up. up=0 means down. ×100 = percentage

Prometheus Storage & Retention — What Happens to Old Metrics?

Prometheus stores time-series data in its TSDB (Time Series Database). As a CNPA, you need to understand the storage model to plan capacity and retention policies:

💾
Local TSDB Storage

• Prometheus stores 2-hour blocks of compressed time-series data on local disk.
• Default retention: 15 days (--storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d).
• Retention size cap: --storage.tsdb.retention.size=50GB (auto-deletes oldest when exceeded).
• anihpj: 200 metrics × 15s scrape = ~2GB/day. 15 days = 30GB. Plan disk accordingly.

☁️
Long-Term Storage (Thanos/Cortex)

• Prometheus alone is NOT for long-term retention (months/years).
• Thanos: Sidecar uploads TSDB blocks to S3. Query layer merges local + remote data. Enables global view across clusters.
• Cortex/Mimir: Horizontally-scalable Prometheus as a service. Separates ingestion, storage, and querying.
• CNPA note: For platform observability at scale, pair Prometheus with Thanos or Mimir for long-term storage and multi-cluster querying.

ServiceMonitor — How Prometheus Discovers Your Pods in Kubernetes

Prometheus doesn't need a static list of targets. It uses ServiceMonitors (Prometheus Operator CRD) to auto-discover pods via Kubernetes labels. This is how the platform golden path auto-configures monitoring for every new service:

anihpj-api-servicemonitor.yaml 
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    team: jobpost-team
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api        # Find Services with this label
  endpoints:
  - port: http               # Scrape this port
    path: /metrics           # Scrape this path
    interval: 30s            # Every 30 seconds
    scrapeTimeout: 10s       # Timeout after 10s
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
    - anihpj-prod

# HOW IT WORKS:
# 1. ServiceMonitor CR created → Prometheus Operator detects it
# 2. Prometheus reads the ServiceMonitor spec
# 3. Prometheus finds all Services matching `app: anihpj-api`
# 4. Prometheus scrapes :8000/metrics every 30s
# 5. No manual Prometheus config changes needed — fully declarative!
#
# GOLDEN PATH: Backstage scaffolder creates this ServiceMonitor
# automatically for every new service. Zero config for developers.
💡 Prometheus PULL vs PUSH — CNPA Exam Distinction

PULL (Prometheus): Prometheus reaches INTO your pods. Requires: /metrics endpoint, network access, service discovery. Benefits: simpler app code, Prometheus controls scrape frequency, easy to detect if a target is down (up=0).

PUSH (Datadog/CloudWatch/InfluxDB): App sends metrics TO the monitoring system. Requires: monitoring SDK in app code, API keys, network egress. Benefits: works for short-lived jobs (CronJobs, batch), no ingress needed.

CNPA Rule: Use Prometheus PULL for long-running services (Deployments, StatefulSets). Use Pushgateway or OTel Collector for short-lived jobs (CronJobs). Never use Pushgateway for long-running services — it's an anti-pattern.

Alertmanager + PrometheusRule — From Metrics to PagerDuty

Prometheus metrics are only useful if they trigger ACTION. Alertmanager takes alerts from Prometheus, groups them to prevent alert storms, routes them to the right team, and handles silencing during maintenance. Here's the complete alerting pipeline for anihpj:

anihpj-alert-rules.yaml — PrometheusRule CRD 
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-alerts
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  groups:
  - name: anihpj-api
    rules:
    - alert: HighErrorRate
      expr: |
        rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api",
          status=~"5.."}[5m])
        /
        rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"}[5m])
        > 0.05
      for: 5m                    # Must persist 5 min (avoid flapping)
      labels:
        severity: critical
        team: jobpost-team
      annotations:
        summary: "anihpj-api error rate > 5%"
        description: "Error rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}"
        runbook_url: "https://backstage.anihpj.io/runbooks/high-error-rate"

    - alert: HighLatency
      expr: |
        histogram_quantile(0.95,
          rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{
            app="anihpj-api"}[5m]))
        > 0.5
      for: 10m
      labels:
        severity: warning
        team: jobpost-team
      annotations:
        summary: "anihpj-api P95 latency > 500ms"

    - alert: MemorySaturation
      expr: |
        container_memory_working_set_bytes{
          pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}
        /
        container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{
          pod=~"anihpj-api-.*"}
        > 0.85
      for: 15m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: "anihpj-api memory > 85% — OOM risk"
🔔
Alertmanager Routing — Who Gets Paged?

• Grouping: Multiple alerts → ONE notification (not 50)
• Routing: severity=critical → PagerDuty. severity=warning → Slack #alerts
• Silencing: Mute during planned maintenance windows
• Inhibition: Node down? Don't also page for every pod on that node

📊
Alert Best Practices (CNPA Tested)

• Alert on SYMPTOMS: "Users getting 500s" not "CPU > 80%"
• Include runbook URLs: Every alert links to Backstage resolution guide
• Use `for:` to avoid flapping: 5 min critical, 15 min warning
• Page the RIGHT team: Labels route to the team owning the service

SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets — The "Why" Behind the Alerts

Metrics and alerts only make sense in the context of Service Level Objectives (SLOs). This is the bridge between observability and reliability — heavily tested on CNPA:

📏
SLI — Service Level Indicator (WHAT you measure)

A quantitative measure of service behavior. anihpj: "Proportion of non-5xx requests = 99.7%." PromQL: rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5.."}[28d]) / rate(http_requests_total[28d])

🎯
SLO — Service Level Objective (INTERNAL target)

A target for an SLI. anihpj: "99.9% success over 28 days." This allows 0.1% failure = 43 min downtime/month. Always stricter than the customer-facing SLA.

💰
Error Budget — Your Allowed Failure

1 − SLO = how much unreliability you're ALLOWED. Budget not exhausted → deploy freely. Budget exhausted → FREEZE deployments. Error budgets make speed vs. reliability trade-offs explicit.

📝
SLA — Service Level Agreement (EXTERNAL promise)

A contract with users. anihpj: "99.5% uptime guaranteed." SLA (99.5%) is LOOSER than SLO (99.9%) — this gives buffer to fix issues BEFORE the SLA is breached. Breach → refunds.

Prometheus Federation — Scaling Metrics Across Multiple Clusters

As your platform grows beyond a single cluster, you need multi-cluster metrics aggregation. Prometheus Federation creates a hierarchical architecture: regional Prometheus instances scrape local targets at high resolution, and a global Prometheus federates aggregated metrics from all regions:

PROMETHEUS FEDERATION — Multi-Cluster Metrics Aggregation
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │           GLOBAL PROMETHEUS (Aggregator)                   │ │
  │  │  • Scrapes /federate from regional Prometheis             │ │
  │  │  • Aggregates: sum(rate(...)) by (cluster)                │ │
  │  │  • Long retention: 1 year (Thanos/Mimir backed)           │ │
  │  └───────┬───────────────────┬───────────────────┬───────────┘ │
  │          │ /federate         │ /federate         │ /federate     │
  │  ┌───────▼──────┐  ┌────────▼──────┐  ┌────────▼──────┐       │
  │  │ REGIONAL     │  │ REGIONAL      │  │ REGIONAL      │       │
  │  │ PROMETHEUS   │  │ PROMETHEUS    │  │ PROMETHEUS    │       │
  │  │ (us-east-1)  │  │ (eu-west-1)   │  │ (ap-southeast)│       │
  │  │ 15d, 15s     │  │ 15d, 15s      │  │ 15d, 15s      │       │
  │  │ scrape       │  │ scrape        │  │ scrape        │       │
  │  └──────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 FEDERATION RULES: Regional = high-res, short retention.    │
  │     Global = aggregated, long retention. Only federate what's   │
  │     needed. Alternative: Thanos for global query without fed.   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prometheus High Availability — Running Redundant Instances

🔄
HA Pair (Simple)

Run 2 identical Prometheus pods. Both scrape same targets independently. Grafana queries both — auto-fallback if one fails. No single point of monitoring failure.

⚡
Thanos HA (Advanced)

Thanos sidecar uploads TSDB blocks to S3. Thanos Querier deduplicates from both replicas. If one dies, data still in S3. Enables global multi-cluster query.

7.3 Logs with Loki — "Like Prometheus, But for Logs"

Loki is a horizontally-scalable, highly-available log aggregation system inspired by Prometheus. It's designed to be cost-effective and easy to operate — unlike Elasticsearch, Loki does NOT index the full text of logs. It only indexes metadata (labels), storing the actual log content compressed in object storage (S3, GCS). This makes Loki dramatically cheaper for high-volume logging:

📖 Loki vs Elasticsearch — The Cost Difference

Elasticsearch: Indexes EVERY word of EVERY log line. Powerful full-text search, but the index is often LARGER than the raw logs. Expensive at scale — 1TB of logs can require 1.5TB of index storage.

Loki: Only indexes LABELS (app="anihpj-api", env="prod"). The log content is stored compressed in object storage (10× compression typical). 1TB of logs ≈ 100GB stored. Query by labels first, then grep the content. Slightly slower for pure full-text search, but 90% cheaper.

Loki Architecture — Label-Based Log Aggregation

LOKI ARCHITECTURE — Log Aggregation for Platforms
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐                        │
  │  │  anihpj-api    │  │  anihpj-web    │   ← Pods write to      │
  │  │  stdout/stderr │  │  stdout/stderr │     stdout/stderr      │
  │  └───────┬────────┘  └───────┬────────┘                        │
  │          │                   │                                  │
  │  ┌───────▼───────────────────▼────────┐                        │
  │  │      PROMTAIL (Log Collector)       │  ← Runs as DaemonSet  │
  │  │  • Tails container logs             │    on every node      │
  │  │  • Adds K8s metadata as labels:     │                       │
  │  │    {app="anihpj-api",               │                       │
  │  │     namespace="anihpj-prod",        │                       │
  │  │     pod="anihpj-api-7",             │                       │
  │  │     container="api"}               │                       │
  │  └───────────────────┬─────────────────┘                       │
  │                      │ PUSH logs (gRPC)                        │
  │  ┌───────────────────▼─────────────────┐                       │
  │  │              LOKI                    │                       │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  │                       │
  │  │  │Ingester  │  │ Object Store    │  │                       │
  │  │  │(indexes  │─▶│ (S3/GCS — cheap │  │                       │
  │  │  │ labels   │  │  compressed     │  │                       │
  │  │  │ only!)   │  │  logs)          │  │                       │
  │  │  └──────────┘  └─────────────────┘  │                       │
  │  └───────────────────┬─────────────────┘                       │
  │                      │ LogQL queries                           │
  │  ┌───────────────────▼─────────────────┐                       │
  │  │             GRAFANA                  │                       │
  │  │  {app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR"      │                       │
  │  │  → Shows all ERROR logs from API    │                       │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘                       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY INSIGHT: Loki indexes LABELS only (cheap). Log content  │
  │     stored compressed in S3 (cheap). Query: filter by labels    │
  │     FIRST, then grep content. Fast AND cost-effective.          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Loki Multi-Tenancy — Isolating Logs Per Team in a Shared Loki

In a multi-tenant platform, you don't want Team A seeing Team B's logs. Loki supports multi-tenancy through a header-based isolation model — one Loki instance serves all teams, but each team only sees their own data:

🏢
How Loki Multi-Tenancy Works

• Each team gets a unique tenant ID (e.g., "team-anihpj", "team-ml")
• Grafana sends X-Scope-OrgID: team-anihpj header with every query
• Loki stores data per-tenant internally — completely isolated
• Team A's LogQL queries CANNOT see Team B's logs
• One Loki cluster serves all teams — no per-team Loki instances needed

⚖️
Enforcing Limits Per Tenant

• Ingestion rate limit: 10MB/s per tenant (prevents one team from overwhelming Loki)
• Query limit: Max 100 concurrent queries per tenant
• Retention per tenant: Team-anihpj: 30 days. Team-ml (compliance): 365 days
• CNPA pattern: The platform team configures tenant limits. Teams get isolated log views without running their own Loki.

Structured Logging — Why JSON Logs Matter for Platforms

Plain text logs are hard to parse. Structured logging (JSON format) makes every field queryable. This is a platform requirement — your golden paths should configure structured logging by default:

anihpj — Structured JSON Logging (Python) 
# settings.py — Django structured logging config
LOGGING = {
    'version': 1,
    'formatters': {
        'json': {
            '()': 'pythonjsonlogger.jsonlogger.JsonFormatter',
            'format': '%(timestamp)s %(level)s %(name)s %(message)s'
        }
    },
    'handlers': {
        'console': {
            'class': 'logging.StreamHandler',
            'formatter': 'json',
            'stream': 'ext://sys.stdout'  # → captured by K8s
        }
    },
    'root': {'handlers': ['console'], 'level': 'INFO'}
}

# Produces structured logs (one JSON object per line):
# {"timestamp":"2026-06-15T14:30:00Z","level":"ERROR",
#  "name":"anihpj.jobpost.views","message":"DB connection timeout",
#  "duration_ms":320,"endpoint":"/api/jobs/",
#  "db_host":"10.244.2.10","retries":3}

# Now in LogQL you can query specific fields:
# {app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR" | json | duration_ms > 200
# → "Show all ERROR logs where duration_ms exceeded 200"

LogQL — Querying Logs Like PromQL

LogQL is Loki's query language, designed to feel familiar to PromQL users. Here are the essential patterns:

LogQL — Essential Log Queries for Platform Engineering 
# ─── FILTER BY LABELS (fast — uses index) ───
{app="anihpj-api", namespace="anihpj-prod"}
# → All logs from anihpj-api in production

# ─── FULL-TEXT SEARCH (slower — scans content) ───
{app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR"
# → Logs containing "ERROR" (case-sensitive)

# ─── NEGATIVE SEARCH ───
{app="anihpj-api"} != "healthz"
# → Exclude health check noise

# ─── REGEX SEARCH ───
{app="anihpj-api"} |~ "(?i)timeout|connection refused"
# → Logs matching regex (case-insensitive)

# ─── PARSE JSON + FILTER ───
{app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR" | json | duration_ms > 200
# → Parse JSON, filter where duration_ms > 200

# ─── AGGREGATE: Error count over time ───
rate({app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR" [5m])
# → How many ERROR logs per second?

# ─── CORRELATE WITH METRICS (in Grafana) ───
# Click a spike in the Prometheus error rate graph →
# Grafana automatically shows the Loki logs for that time window.
# This is the POWER of unified observability.

7.4 Distributed Tracing — Following a Request Across Services

Distributed tracing is what makes microservices debuggable. When a single user request touches 5 different services (web → api → db → redis → back), tracing follows that request end-to-end, showing exactly where time was spent and where the bottleneck is:

📖 Tracing Concepts — Spans, Traces, Context Propagation

Span: A single unit of work with a start time, duration, and metadata. "DB query: SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE... took 320ms."

Trace: A collection of spans that form the complete journey of one request. All spans in a trace share the same Trace ID.

Context Propagation: The mechanism by which Trace IDs are passed between services. Via HTTP headers: traceparent: 00-abc123def456-01. Every service adds this header to outgoing requests, creating a connected chain of spans.

Distributed Tracing — Following an anihpj Request

DISTRIBUTED TRACING — anihpj Request Waterfall
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  TRACE ID: abc123def456 (same ID across ALL spans!)             │
  │                                                                 │
  │  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────▶   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Ingress    ██ 2ms                                              │
  │             └─┐                                                 │
  │  anihpj-web   ██████ 15ms                                       │
  │               │  └─┐                                            │
  │  anihpj-api     ██████████████████ 45ms                         │
  │                 │       │                                       │
  │  anihpj-db        ████████████████████████████████████ 320ms   │
  │                   │                                             │
  │  anihpj-redis      ██ 2ms                                       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
  │  TOTAL: 382ms                                                   │
  │  BOTTLENECK: anihpj-db query (320ms = 84% of total time!)       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🔍 TRACING ANSWERS QUESTIONS METRICS CAN'T:                     │
  │  • "The P95 latency is 500ms — WHICH service is slow?"          │
  │  • "Is the DB slow for ALL queries or just this one endpoint?"  │
  │  • "Is the Redis call happening IN PARALLEL or SEQUENTIAL?"     │
  │  • "Which downstream service is causing the cascade failure?"   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE COMPLETE OBSERVABILITY STORY:                           │
  │  • Metrics: "500 error rate spiked to 15%" (WHAT, when)        │
  │  • Logs: "DB connection timeout at 10.244.2.10" (WHY)          │
  │  • Traces: "The /api/jobs/ query took 320ms in the DB —         │
  │     that's where 84% of time is spent" (WHERE specifically)     │
  │  • Events: "Deployment scaled down at 14:28 — fewer DB         │
  │     connections available" (WHAT triggered it)                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Context Propagation — How Traces Connect Across Services

For tracing to work, every service in the chain must pass the Trace ID forward. This is context propagation — and it's why you need instrumentation in ALL your services, not just one:

CONTEXT PROPAGATION — How Trace IDs Flow Through Services
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  Browser                                                       │
  │    │ GET /api/jobs/                                            │
  │    │ (no trace ID yet)                                         │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  anihpj-web                                                    │
  │    │ Creates Span 1 (15ms) + generates Trace ID: abc123        │
  │    │ Forwards Trace ID via HTTP header:                        │
  │    │   traceparent: 00-abc123-0000000000000001-01              │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  anihpj-api                                                    │
  │    │ Reads Trace ID from header: abc123                        │
  │    │ Creates Span 2 (45ms) — CHILD of Span 1                   │
  │    │ Forwards Trace ID to DB:                                  │
  │    │   traceparent: 00-abc123-0000000000000002-01              │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  anihpj-db                                                     │
  │    │ Reads Trace ID: abc123                                    │
  │    │ Creates Span 3 (320ms) — CHILD of Span 2                  │
  │    │ Returns result. Span 3 ends.                              │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  anihpj-api (continues)                                        │
  │    │ Calls Redis with same Trace ID:                           │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  anihpj-redis                                                  │
  │    │ Creates Span 4 (2ms) — CHILD of Span 2                    │
  │    │ Returns. Span 4 ends.                                     │
  │    ▼                                                           │
  │  Response flows back: web (Span 1 ends) → Browser              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  RESULT: All 4 spans share Trace ID abc123.                     │
  │  Tempo/Jaeger reconstructs the waterfall from these spans.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💡 CNPA Insight: If even ONE service in the chain doesn't propagate the Trace ID, the trace BREAKS. You'll see Span 1 → Span 2 → (gap) → Span 4. This is why platform golden paths must include OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation for ALL services — manual instrumentation guarantees gaps.

Trace Sampling — Why You Can't Keep 100% of Traces

At scale, keeping every trace is prohibitively expensive. anihpj handles 10,000 requests/second — that's 10,000 traces/second = 864 million traces/day. Sampling decides which traces to keep. The CNPA exam tests the difference between head-based and tail-based sampling:

❌ Head-Based Sampling (Jaeger Default)

Decision made UPFRONT — at the START of the trace, before you know if it'll error.

Example: "Keep 10% of all traces randomly."

Problem: If your error rate is 0.1%, then 99.9% of the traces you KEEP are successful ones. The ONE trace with the critical error? 90% chance you THREW IT AWAY because the sampling decision was made before the error occurred.

Result: "We know we had errors, but all the error traces were sampled out. We can't debug the incident."

✅ Tail-Based Sampling (Tempo Default)

Decision made AFTER — at the END of the trace, when you KNOW if it errored or was slow.

Example: "Keep 100% of traces with errors or latency > 500ms. Keep 10% of successful, fast traces."

Benefit: You NEVER lose an error trace. Every incident is fully debuggable. You still save 90% on storage because most traces are successful and sampled down.

Result: "We had 47 errors. Here are ALL 47 traces showing exactly what happened. Here's the root cause."

Tempo vs Jaeger — Choosing a Trace Backend

Both Tempo and Jaeger store and query traces. The CNPA exam expects you to know when to choose which:

AspectTempo (Grafana Labs)Jaeger (CNCF Graduated)
StorageObject storage (S3/GCS) — cheap, scalable, no local disks neededElasticsearch, Cassandra, or badger — more expensive, higher ops burden
SearchSearch by Trace ID + tags. NO full-text search (by design, like Loki)Full-text search via Elasticsearch backend (more powerful, more expensive)
IntegrationNative Grafana integration. Click metric spike → see traces automaticallySeparate Jaeger UI. Can integrate with Grafana but less seamless
SamplingTail-based sampling — keep 100% of errors, sample successes at 10%Head-based sampling only — random % upfront, might miss rare errors
Best forPlatforms using Grafana stack (Prometheus + Loki + Tempo). Cost-sensitive.Standalone tracing needs. When full-text search is required.
CNPA ChoiceTempo — integrates natively with the Grafana observability stack. Object storage is dramatically cheaper. Tail-based sampling ensures you never miss error traces. Jaeger is solid but Tempo is purpose-built for the Prometheus + Loki + Grafana ecosystem.

7.5 Dashboards with Grafana — Unified Visualization

Grafana is the universal visualization layer that brings metrics, logs, and traces together in a single pane of glass. It connects to Prometheus (metrics), Loki (logs), and Tempo/Jaeger (traces) — allowing you to seamlessly navigate between them during incident response:

📖 Grafana's Role in the Platform

Grafana doesn't STORE data — it VISUALIZES data from multiple sources. This is critical: Prometheus stores metrics, Loki stores logs, Tempo stores traces. Grafana queries all three and presents them in unified dashboards. For a CNPA, Grafana is where you build the platform overview dashboard that every team uses to monitor their services.

USE Metrics — Beyond RED for Infrastructure Monitoring

RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) cover APPLICATION health. USE metrics cover INFRASTRUCTURE health — the resources your application runs on. Every CNPA platform dashboard should include both:

⚡
UTILIZATION — How much is being used?

CPU: cpu_usage_percent → 65% (normal)
Memory: memory_usage → 412MB / 512Mi (80%)
Disk: disk_usage → 45GB / 100GB (45%)
Network: network_bytes → 850 Mbps
Alert when: Any resource > 80% utilization → scale up before saturation.

🛑
SATURATION — How much "extra work" is queued?

CPU: cpu_throttled_seconds → 0.1s/s (1% throttle — OK)
Memory: oom_killed_total → 0 (no OOMs)
Disk: disk_io_queue_depth → 3 (normal)
Alert when: CPU throttling > 5%, OOM events > 0, or IO queue growing exponentially.

❌
ERRORS — How many infrastructure failures?

Node: node_errors → 0 (healthy)
Disk: disk_read_errors → 0
Network: network_drops → 12 (12 packets dropped — investigate)
Alert when: Any error counter > 0 — infrastructure errors are almost always serious.

💡 The CNPA Dashboard Golden Path

Every service created via the platform golden path should get a PRE-BUILT Grafana dashboard auto-provisioned. The dashboard includes: RED metrics (rate, errors, latency), USE metrics (CPU, memory, disk), application-specific panels (DB connections, queue depth), and links to Loki logs and Tempo traces. Developers should NEVER need to build a dashboard from scratch — that's cognitive load the platform absorbs.

Grafana Provisioning as Code — Dashboards from Git, Not UI Clicks

In a GitOps-managed platform, Grafana dashboards should be version-controlled in Git and auto-provisioned — never created by clicking through the Grafana UI. This ensures dashboards survive Grafana pod restarts and can be reviewed like any other code change:

Grafana Dashboard Provisioning — GitOps Pattern 
# ─── Dashboard Provisioning ConfigMap (auto-loaded by Grafana) ───
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: grafana-dashboard-anihpj-api
  namespace: platform-monitoring
  labels:
    grafana_dashboard: "1"       # Grafana auto-discovers this label
data:
  anihpj-api-overview.json: |    # Full dashboard JSON (exported from Grafana)
    {
      "title": "anihpj-api Overview",
      "uid": "anihpj-api-red",
      "panels": [
        {
          "title": "Request Rate",
          "targets": [{
            "expr": "rate(http_requests_total{app=\"anihpj-api\"}[5m])"
          }]
        },
        {
          "title": "Error Rate",
          "targets": [{
            "expr": "rate(http_requests_total{app=\"anihpj-api\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total{app=\"anihpj-api\"}[5m])"
          }]
        },
        {
          "title": "P95 Latency",
          "targets": [{
            "expr": "histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{app=\"anihpj-api\"}[5m]))"
          }]
        }
      ]
    }

# HOW IT WORKS:
# 1. Platform team commits dashboard JSON to Git
# 2. ArgoCD syncs ConfigMap to cluster
# 3. Grafana sidecar watches for ConfigMaps with label `grafana_dashboard: "1"`
# 4. Dashboard auto-appears in Grafana — no manual import
# 5. Update dashboard = update JSON in Git = ArgoCD syncs = Grafana updates
#
# GOLDEN PATH: Backstage scaffolder creates this ConfigMap automatically
# for every new service. Developers never touch Grafana UI for dashboards.

7.6 OpenTelemetry — The Unified Observability Standard

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a CNCF project that provides a UNIFIED standard for generating, collecting, and exporting telemetry data (metrics, logs, and traces). Think of it as "one SDK to instrument, send to any backend" — no vendor lock-in, no rewriting instrumentation when you switch monitoring tools:

📖 OpenTelemetry Defined

OpenTelemetry decouples instrumentation (how you generate telemetry) from backend (where you send it). Today you send to Prometheus + Loki + Tempo. Tomorrow you switch to Datadog — just change the Exporter configuration. Zero application code changes. This vendor neutrality is why OTel is the CNPA-recommended standard for platform observability.

OpenTelemetry Pipeline — Receive → Process → Export

OPENTELEMETRY — The Unified Observability Pipeline
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  anihpj APPLICATION (with OTel Python SDK)                 │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Auto-instrumentation (NO code changes needed!):           │ │
  │  │  • Django requests → Traces + Metrics                     │ │
  │  │  • PostgreSQL queries → Spans + Duration                  │ │
  │  │  • Redis calls → Spans                                   │ │
  │  │  • Python logging → Structured Logs                       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ALL telemetry flows via OTLP protocol (gRPC)             │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                             │ OTLP (gRPC)                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │        OPENTELEMETRY COLLECTOR (Your Data Pipeline)        │ │
  │  │                                                            │ │
  │  │  RECEIVE ──▶ PROCESS ──▶ EXPORT                           │ │
  │  │  (OTLP,     (batch,     ┌──────────────────┐              │ │
  │  │   Jaeger,    filter,    │ Prometheus        │ ← Metrics   │ │
  │  │   Zipkin)    sample,    ├──────────────────┤              │ │
  │  │              enrich)    │ Loki              │ ← Logs      │ │
  │  │                         ├──────────────────┤              │ │
  │  │                         │ Tempo             │ ← Traces    │ │
  │  │                         ├──────────────────┤              │ │
  │  │                         │ Jaeger (backup)   │              │ │
  │  │                         └──────────────────┘              │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY BENEFIT: Switch backends WITHOUT changing app code      │
  │  • Today:  Prometheus + Loki + Tempo (open source, free)       │
  │  • Tomorrow: Datadog (just change Exporter config!)             │
  │  • Next year: NewRelic (again, just change Exporter!)           │
  │  • The instrumentation code NEVER changes.                      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Auto-Instrumentation — Observability Without Code Changes

One of OTel's most powerful features for platform engineering: you can instrument an entire application with ZERO code changes. The CNPA golden path should include OTel auto-instrumentation by default:

anihpj — OpenTelemetry Auto-Instrumentation 
# Dockerfile — Add OTel auto-instrumentation (no code changes!)
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN pip install opentelemetry-distro \
    opentelemetry-exporter-otlp \
    opentelemetry-instrumentation-django \
    opentelemetry-instrumentation-psycopg2 \
    opentelemetry-instrumentation-redis
RUN opentelemetry-bootstrap --action=install

# Kubernetes Deployment — Inject OTel via environment variables
env:
- name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
  value: "anihpj-api"
- name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
  value: "http://otel-collector.observability:4317"
- name: OTEL_PYTHON_LOGGING_AUTO_INSTRUMENTATION_ENABLED
  value: "true"

# RESULT:
# • All Django requests → auto-traced
# • All PostgreSQL queries → auto-traced  
# • All Redis calls → auto-traced
# • All Python logs → auto-correlated with traces
# • ZERO application code changed!

The 4 Golden Signals — What Google SRE Taught Us About Monitoring

Beyond RED and USE metrics, Google's SRE book defines 4 Golden Signals that every platform service should monitor. These form the foundation of your alerting strategy:

📈
1. Latency — How long does it take?

Measure: P50 (typical), P95 (alert on), P99 (investigate).
anihpj: P50=120ms (normal), P95=245ms (OK), P99=580ms (borderline).
Alert: P95 > 500ms for 5 minutes.
Why P95 not average: Average hides outliers. If 95% of users are fast but 5% are 10 seconds, the average might look fine — but 5% of users are suffering.

📊
2. Traffic — How much demand?

Measure: Requests per second, active connections.
anihpj: 152 req/sec (web), 89 req/sec (api).
Alert: Traffic drops 50% from baseline (service dead?) OR traffic spikes 300% (DDoS? Black Friday?).
Use for: Capacity planning. "We'll need 2× servers by next quarter if this trend continues."

❌
3. Errors — How many failures?

Measure: 5xx errors, timeouts, dropped connections.
anihpj: 0.3% error rate (47 errors / 15,231 requests).
Alert: Error rate > 1% (SLO breach imminent). Error rate > 5% (CRITICAL — incident).
Explicit vs implicit: 500 = explicit error. 200 but with wrong data = implicit error (harder to catch).

🛑
4. Saturation — How "full" is the service?

Measure: CPU %, memory %, DB connections, queue depth.
anihpj: CPU 65% (OK), memory 80% (watch), DB connections 47/100 (OK), Celery queue 12 (OK).
Alert: Any resource > 80% (WARNING), > 90% (CRITICAL).
Leading indicator: Saturation predicts problems BEFORE they become errors. If CPU is at 90%, errors are coming.

Observability Stack Comparison — Open Source vs Commercial

As a CNPA, you'll need to justify platform tooling choices. Here's how the open-source CNCF stack compares to commercial alternatives for anihpj-scale deployments:

CapabilityOpen Source (CNCF Stack)Commercial (Datadog / New Relic)
MetricsPrometheus — free, self-managed, PULL model, PromQLVendor SDK + agent — PUSH model, proprietary query language
LogsLoki — label-indexed, S3-backed, LogQL. ~$50/month for 1TB ingestionFull-text indexed, proprietary search. ~$1,500/month for 1TB ingestion
TracesTempo — S3-backed, tail-based sampling. ~$30/month for 1M spansFull-text trace search. ~$500/month for 1M spans
DashboardsGrafana — free, unified, community dashboards (10,000+ on grafana.com)Built-in dashboards. Less customizable. Vendor-specific.
Vendor Lock-inNone — OTel standard. Switch backends anytime.Proprietary agents + APIs. Migration is painful and expensive.
Operational BurdenYOU manage Prometheus, Loki, Tempo (upgrades, scaling, HA)Vendor manages everything — zero ops burden
Best ForPlatform teams with K8s expertise. Cost-sensitive. Multi-cloud.Teams prioritizing operational simplicity. Single-vendor preference.
anihpj Monthly Cost~$200 (infra: 3 nodes for monitoring stack)~$4,000+ (per-host pricing for 20 nodes)

💡 CNPA Insight: The CNCF open-source observability stack (Prometheus + Loki + Tempo + Grafana + OTel) costs roughly 5% of equivalent commercial tools at scale. The trade-off: you need K8s operational expertise. For a CNPA-certified platform engineer, this is exactly your skill set — making the open-source stack the clear winner for most platform teams.

7.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of observability fundamentals, Prometheus, Loki, tracing, Grafana, and OpenTelemetry.

Observability Maturity Model — Where Is Your Platform?

Observability isn't binary (you have it or you don't). Platforms evolve through stages. The CNPA exam tests your ability to assess observability maturity and identify what's needed to reach the next level:

👀
LEVEL 1
REACTIVE (Manual)

SSH into pods, tail logs. No dashboards. "Users report issues before we know."

MTTR: HOURS
📊
LEVEL 2
MONITORED (Metrics Only)

Prometheus + Grafana. Basic RED dashboards. Alert on thresholds. Know WHEN issues happen.

MTTR: 30 MIN
🔍
LEVEL 3 ← CNPA
OBSERVABLE (Full Stack)

Metrics + Logs + Traces. Loki + Tempo + OTel. Unified Grafana. RED + USE + Golden Signals.

MTTR: 5 MIN
🤖
LEVEL 4
PREDICTIVE (AI-Driven)

AIOps anomaly detection. Predict issues before they occur. Auto-remediation of known patterns.

MTTR: 1 MIN

The Observability Incident Response Flow — From Alert to Resolution

Here's how the three pillars work together during a real incident. This is the flow CNPA platform engineers should design for:

OBSERVABILITY INCIDENT RESPONSE — Metrics → Logs → Traces → Fix
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⏰ 14:30:05 — ALERT FIRES (Prometheus → Alertmanager → PagerDuty)│
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Prometheus detects: error_rate{anihpj-api} = 15% (SLO=1%)│ │
  │  │  Alertmanager: severity=critical → PagerDuty pages Alice  │ │
  │  │  Alice opens Grafana on her phone (mobile dashboard)      │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                         │ 30 seconds                             │
  │  ⏰ 14:30:35 — DIAGNOSE (Grafana Unified View)                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Grafana: Error rate spike at 14:30. Click the spike.     │ │
  │  │  Grafana auto-navigates to Loki logs for that time window:│ │
  │  │  {app="anihpj-api"} |= "ERROR" → "DB connection timeout   │ │
  │  │  at 10.244.2.10:5432 — pool exhausted (100/100)"         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                         │ 60 seconds                             │
  │  ⏰ 14:31:35 — PINPOINT (Distributed Tracing)                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Grafana: Click "View Trace" on a failed request.         │ │
  │  │  Tempo waterfall shows: /api/jobs/search → DB query 2.3s  │ │
  │  │  (normally 45ms!) — new search endpoint creating a fresh  │ │
  │  │  DB connection per request instead of using the pool.     │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                         │ 120 seconds                            │
  │  ⏰ 14:33:35 — FIX & VERIFY                                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │

  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │

Observability Q1 of 10
A developer sees "500 error rate spiked to 15%." They open the Prometheus dashboard and see high error rates. What observability pillar should they use NEXT to understand WHY?
A) More metrics — add a counter for each error type
B) Logs — check Loki for ERROR-level logs during the spike to find the root cause message
C) Events — check what Kubernetes events fired at that time
D) Traces — follow a failing request through all services
✅ Correct Answer: B — Logs tell you WHY

Metrics (Prometheus) tell you WHAT and WHEN (error rate spiked). The NEXT step is Logs (Loki) to understand WHY — "DB connection timeout" or "null pointer exception." After you know what AND why, Traces (Tempo) show WHERE in the call chain the problem originates. The observability workflow: Metrics alert → Logs explain → Traces pinpoint.

Observability Q2 of 10
Which Prometheus metric type should you use to track the total number of HTTP requests served by anihpj-api since startup?
A) Counter — http_requests_total (only increases, perfect for counting)
B) Gauge — http_requests_current (can go up and down)
C) Histogram — http_requests_bucket (bucketed observations)
D) Summary — http_requests_summary (client-side quantiles)
✅ Correct Answer: A — Counter

Counters only increase (or reset to 0 on restart). They're perfect for counting cumulative events: total requests, total errors, total bytes sent. Use rate() to convert to per-second.
